scenarios.title: The 99.9% Question
scenarios.situation: A vendor contract promises 99.9% monthly uptime. The operations lead needs the allowed downtime budget in minutes to set alerting thresholds.
scenarios.prompt: What is the monthly downtime budget for 99.9%?
evidence: 0.1% of a 30-day month = 0.001 x 30 x 24 x 60 minutes
choices: Zero - 99.9% means no downtime is allowed
scenarios.why: 0.001 x 30 x 24 x 60 = 43.2 minutes (about 43.8 with a 30.44-day average month). Each additional nine divides the budget by ten: 99.95% is ~21.6 min, 99.99% is ~4.3 min. Knowing the budget in minutes is what makes the SLA operationally real.
scenarios.hint: Convert the 0.1% allowance into minutes over 30 days. What does each extra 'nine' do to the budget?

scenarios.title: GB vs GiB Quote
scenarios.situation: Two storage vendors quote '500' units of capacity. Vendor A means decimal gigabytes (500 x 1000^3 bytes); Vendor B's system bills binary gibibytes. The prices look identical per 'unit.'
scenarios.prompt: How should the quotes be compared?
evidence:
Vendor A: 500 GB decimal | System billing: GiB binary
500 x 1000^3 / 1024^3 = ~465.66 GiB
choices: Convert both to the same unit first - Vendor A's 500 GB is only ~465.66 GiB of billable capacity
Treat the units as equal - GB and GiB are interchangeable
Pick whichever quote has the bigger number
Ignore the units - capacity is capacity
scenarios.why: Decimal GB and binary GiB differ by about 7% per unit - 500 GB is only ~465.66 GiB. Comparing prices per mismatched unit hides a real capacity shortfall that appears on the first invoice. Dimensional analysis (carrying units through the computation) catches this before signing.
scenarios.hint: What does the conversion in the evidence say about the actual capacity you would be billed for?

scenarios.title: Burning Down the Backlog
scenarios.situation: The support queue grows by 8 tickets a day: 40 arrive, 32 get resolved. Management proposes mandatory overtime 'until the backlog clears.'
scenarios.prompt: What does the math say about the overtime plan?
choices: Overtime cannot clear it sustainably - throughput must meet or exceed the 40/day arrival rate, or the queue grows forever
Overtime will clear the 400-ticket backlog in 50 days
Hire one more agent without checking the numbers - headcount always fixes queues
Close the oldest tickets unresolved to reset the backlog to zero
scenarios.why: A queue with arrival rate exceeding service rate grows without bound - that is queueing theory, not effort. At +8/day, the backlog never shrinks no matter how long overtime lasts; it only pauses the growth while burning out the team. The fix is structural: raise sustained throughput to >= 40/day (staffing, automation, deflection) or reduce arrivals.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the +8/day gap during overtime, and what happens the day overtime stops?

scenarios.title: 50 to 75
scenarios.situation: A dashboard shows on-call incidents rising from 50 to 75 per month. One engineer reports 'a 25% increase'; another says 'incidents nearly doubled.'
choices: A 50% increase - 25 additional incidents on a base of 50, i.e., 25 percentage points of the original
A 25% increase - the count rose by 25
It nearly doubled - 75 is close to 100
A 75% increase - the new total is 75
scenarios.why: Percent change is (new - old) / old = 25/50 = 50%. 'Rose by 25' confuses the absolute change with the percent change; 75 is 1.5x the original, not nearly double. Percent change vs percentage points vs absolute change are three different statements - the dashboard should label which one it shows.
scenarios.hint: Percent change divides by the starting value. What is 25 divided by 50?

scenarios.title: Reorder Point
scenarios.situation: A data center stocks replacement SSDs: usage is 20 per day, supplier lead time is 5 days, and safety stock is set at 30 drives. Stockouts halt server repairs.
scenarios.prompt: At what inventory level should the reorder be triggered?
evidence: usage: 20/day | lead time: 5 days | safety stock: 30
choices: 130 drives - demand during lead time (20 x 5 = 100) plus 30 safety stock
30 drives - reorder when safety stock is all that remains
200 drives - double the last order size for safety
Reorder on the first of every month regardless of level
scenarios.why: The reorder point covers demand during the replenishment lead time plus a buffer: 20/day x 5 days = 100, + 30 safety stock = 130. Ordering at 30 means stockouts during every 5-day lead time; doubling the last order confuses order quantity with order timing; calendar reordering ignores actual consumption.
scenarios.hint: How many drives will be consumed while you wait 5 days for delivery? What must still be on the shelf then?

scenarios.title: Two-Leg Average Speed
scenarios.situation: A courier drives 60 km to a site at 60 km/h and returns the same 60 km at 40 km/h. The dispatcher logs the average speed as 50 km/h (the arithmetic mean).
scenarios.prompt: What is the true average speed for the round trip?
evidence:
outbound: 60 km at 60 km/h = 1.0 h
return: 60 km at 40 km/h = 1.5 h
total: 120 km in 2.5 h
choices: 48 km/h - total distance over total time, i.e., the harmonic mean for equal distances
50 km/h - the arithmetic mean of the two speeds
100 km/h - the sum of the two speeds
scenarios.why: Average speed is total distance / total time = 120 / 2.5 = 48 km/h. The arithmetic mean (50) is wrong because more time is spent at the slower speed; for equal distances the correct average of rates is the harmonic mean: 2 / (1/60 + 1/40) = 48. Averaging rates with the arithmetic mean is the classic trap.
scenarios.hint: Average speed is defined as total distance over total time. What does the evidence say those totals are?

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Aleks Ops Math as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Operations Math Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Operations Math is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Operations Math?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Operations Math issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Operations Math is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct approach is as follows: Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Operations Math supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Operations Math failure in Aleks Ops Math.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Operations Math
evidence: All Operations Math components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

Take the full mock on day one to 'see where you stand,' then study randomly.
Read every lesson in all 15 domains first, then attempt scenarios in week three.
Skip lessons entirely and grind drills — speed matters more than understanding.

Keep re-attempting the scenario until you memorize the right answer.
Skip it and move on — one scenario will not decide the assessment.
Look up the answer online and move faster through the rest.

domains.name: Arithmetic Foundations

scenarios.title: The Checkout Line
scenarios.situation: You are splitting a bill and need 8 + 6 / 2 x 3 - 4. Your friend computed left to right and got 17... wait, they got something else. You need the right number.
choices: 13: division and multiplication first (6/2 = 3, 3 x 3 = 9), then 8 + 9 - 4 = 13.
14: divide first, then work left to right ignoring precedence.
scenarios.why: The correct approach honors precedence: multiplication and division (same level, left to right) before addition and subtraction. 6/2 = 3, 3 x 3 = 9, then 8 + 9 - 4 = 13. Left-to-right reading gives 17 (8+6=14, 14/2=7, 7x3=21, 21-4=17) — the classic precedence trap.
scenarios.hint: Which operations does PEMDAS put first here?
objectives: Handle same-level operators left to right

scenarios.title: The Recipe Scale
scenarios.situation: A recipe needs 5/8 of a 96-ounce stock pot filled. Your measuring cup is in ounces.
scenarios.prompt: How many ounces do you need?
scenarios.why: The correct approach divides before multiplying: 96 / 8 = 12, then 12 x 5 = 60. Dividing first keeps the numbers small and exact — multiplying 5 x 96 = 480 first also works but invites arithmetic slips. 'Of' always means multiply with fractions.
scenarios.hint: What does 'of' mean with a fraction, and which order keeps numbers small?

scenarios.title: The Restaurant Tip
scenarios.situation: The bill is $64.50 and you want to leave an 18% tip. You are estimating without a calculator.
scenarios.why: The correct approach converts 18% to 0.18 and multiplies: 0.18 x 64.50 = 11.61. The benchmark decomposition cross-checks it: 10% ($6.45) + 5% ($3.23) + 3% ($1.94) = $11.62, matching within rounding. Estimating first (roughly $11-12) also guards against decimal slips.
scenarios.hint: What is 10% of the bill? Build 18% from there.

scenarios.title: The Signed Expression
scenarios.situation: On a practice test: evaluate (-2)^3 + sqrt(81) - 4^2.
choices: 17: sign errors on the cube and the square.
scenarios.why: The correct approach handles each piece: (-2)^3 = -8 (odd power keeps the negative), sqrt(81) = 9, 4^2 = 16 — then combine left to right: -8 + 9 = 1, 1 - 16 = -15. The traps are (-2)^3 = 8 (sign) and -4^2 confusion, but here the minus is ordinary subtraction of 16.
scenarios.hint: What is the sign of (-2)^3, and what does 4^2 equal?

scenarios.title: The Decimal Product
scenarios.situation: A fabric order: 3.75 yards at $2.40 per yard. Quick mental check before the register total.
choices: 9.00: 3.75 x 2.4 = 9.000 — estimate first: 4 x 2.4 = 9.6, so the answer sits just under 9.6.
scenarios.why: The correct approach estimates first (3.75 rounds to 4; 4 x 2.4 = 9.6, so the answer is near 9) then computes exactly: 375 x 24 = 9000, with 2 + 1 = 3 decimal places -> 9.000. The estimate kills the 90.0 and 0.90 distractors instantly — decimal placement is the whole battle in decimal multiplication.
scenarios.hint: Round first: what is 4 x 2.4? Which choices survive?

scenarios.title: The Mixed Numbers
scenarios.situation: A board is 2 1/2 feet, you add a 1 3/4-foot extension, then trim 3/8 foot off the end.
choices: 4 1/8 feet: added the trim instead of subtracting.
scenarios.why: The correct approach converts to a common denominator of 8: 2 1/2 = 20/8, 1 3/4 = 14/8, trim = 3/8. Then 20 + 14 - 3 = 31, over 8 = 31/8 = 3 7/8 feet. Mixed numbers are safest handled as improper fractions throughout, converting back only at the end.
scenarios.hint: What is the common denominator, and what is 2 1/2 as eighths?

scenarios.title: The Divisibility Test
scenarios.situation: Four invoice numbers: 4,821; 4,820; 7,105; 9,412. A validation rule flags numbers divisible by 3.
choices: 4,820: ends in 0 — that tests divisibility by 5 and 10, not 3.
7,105: ends in 5 — divisible by 5, digit sum 13 rules out 3.
4,821: digit sum 4+8+2+1 = 15, a multiple of 3 — divisible. The others sum to 14, 13, 16 — not multiples of 3.
9,412: even — divisible by 2, but digit sum 16 rules out 3.
scenarios.why: The correct approach applies the digit-sum test: only 4,821's digits sum to a multiple of 3 (15). The distractors exploit rule confusion — evenness tests 2, trailing 0/5 tests 5, but only the digit sum tests 3. One test per rule, no long division needed.
scenarios.hint: What is the divisibility test for 3?

domains.name: Algebra Essentials

scenarios.title: The Unknown Number
scenarios.situation: A shipping formula: 4 times a package weight minus 11 equals 29 pounds of total charge units. What is the weight?
choices: 10: add 11 both sides (4x = 40), divide by 4: x = 10. Check: 4(10) - 11 = 29.
scenarios.why: The correct approach undoes in reverse: +(-11) came last, so add 11 first (4x = 40), then divide by 4 (x = 10). Check: 4(10) - 11 = 40 - 11 = 29. Dividing first or forgetting the division are the two standard slips — the check catches both.
scenarios.hint: What was done to x last? Undo that first.

scenarios.title: The Parentheses Problem
scenarios.situation: Two pricing plans are modeled: 2(x + 3) = 5x - 9, where x is months. When do they cost the same?
scenarios.why: The correct approach distributes first (2x + 6 — not 2x + 3), then collects variables to the side that keeps x positive: 6 + 9 = 5x - 2x gives 15 = 3x, x = 5. Check both original sides: 2(5+3) = 16 and 5(5) - 9 = 16. Negative months would have been the tell for a sign error.
scenarios.hint: After distributing, which side keeps x positive when you collect?

scenarios.title: The Crew Schedule
scenarios.situation: 12 workers finish a job in 8 days. The deadline moves up and you get 16 workers.
scenarios.prompt: How many days will the job take with 16 workers?
choices: 10.67 days: set it up as direct proportion (wrong direction).
6 days: inverse proportion — more workers, fewer days: 12 x 8 = 16 x d, so d = 96/16 = 6.
8 days: assumed workers do not matter.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recognizes inverse proportion: workers x days is constant (the total work), so 12 x 8 = 16 x d and d = 6. Direct setup (12/8 = 16/d) claims more workers take longer — absurd on its face. The sanity check ('should the answer be less than 8?') catches the setup error before any arithmetic.
scenarios.hint: If workers go up, do days go up or down? What setup matches that?
evidence: 12 workers -> 8 days; find days for 16 workers

scenarios.title: The Function Machine
scenarios.situation: A cost model is f(x) = -3x + 14, where x is units in thousands. What is f(-2)?
choices: 8: computed -3(2) + 14, dropping the negative on x.
scenarios.why: The correct approach substitutes carefully: f(-2) = -3(-2) + 14. The product -3 x -2 = +6 (negative times negative), then 6 + 14 = 20. The dominant error is reading -3(-2) as -6 — parentheses around the -2 exist precisely to warn you.
scenarios.hint: What is -3 times -2?

scenarios.title: The Hill Grade
scenarios.situation: A road passes through (1, 5) and (4, 17) on a survey grid (units in hundreds of feet). What is its slope?
choices: 4: m = (17 - 5)/(4 - 1) = 12/3 = 4. The road rises 4 units per 1 across.
3: that is the run, not the slope.
12: forgot to divide by the run.
scenarios.why: The correct approach keeps point order consistent: (17 - 5)/(4 - 1) = 12/3 = 4. Rise over run — 12 up, 3 across. The inversions (3, 12, 1/4) are the three classic slope slips; labeling rise and run before dividing defeats all of them.
scenarios.hint: What is the rise? What is the run? Now divide.

scenarios.title: The Budget Limit
scenarios.situation: A project budget allows 2x + 5 < 17 (thousands), where x is team size. What integer team sizes fit?
scenarios.prompt: Solve 2x + 5 < 17; give the largest integer x.
choices: x > 6: flipped the inequality for no reason.
x < 6, so largest integer is 5: 2x < 12 gives x < 6; integers ..., 4, 5 fit, 6 does not (2(6)+5 = 17, not < 17).
6: missed that the inequality is strict.
scenarios.why: The correct approach solves like an equation (2x < 12, x < 6) — the inequality direction only flips when multiplying/dividing by a negative, which never happens here. Strict < excludes 6 itself: 2(6) + 5 = 17 fails the '< 17' test, so 5 is the largest fitting integer. Boundary testing (plug in 6) is the verification habit.
scenarios.hint: Does x = 6 satisfy the original inequality? Test it.

scenarios.title: The Tiny Measurement
scenarios.situation: A lab instrument measures 0.00045 meters. The report requires scientific notation.
choices: 4.5 x 10^4: positive exponent — that is 45,000, not 0.00045.
45 x 10^-5: equals the right value but is not normalized (45 > 10).
4.5 x 10^-4: coefficient between 1 and 10, decimal moved 4 right so exponent is -4.
0.45 x 10^-4: equals 0.000045 — ten times too small.
scenarios.why: The correct approach moves the decimal 4 places right (small number, negative exponent) and normalizes the coefficient to [1, 10): 4.5 x 10^-4. The 45 x 10^-5 distractor is numerically equal but formally wrong — scientific notation has exactly one non-zero digit before the decimal point, and tests enforce it.
scenarios.hint: Which way did the decimal move, and what must the coefficient look like?

domains.name: Geometry in Practice

scenarios.title: The Fence Bid
scenarios.situation: You are bidding a fence for a rectangular garden 15 ft by 9 ft. The client pays per linear foot.
choices: 48 ft: P = 2(15 + 9) = 48. Perimeter is the fence — add all sides.
135 ft: that is the area (15 x 9) — carpet, not fence.
24 ft: that is half the perimeter.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches the quantity to the formula: fencing follows the boundary, so perimeter P = 2(l + w) = 2(24) = 48 ft. The 135 distractor is the area — the classic perimeter/area swap. Bidding area footage for a fence job underbids catastrophically or overbids embarrassingly.
scenarios.hint: Is a fence around the edge or across the middle?

scenarios.title: The Round Rug
scenarios.situation: A round rug has radius 7 ft. You need its area for the price quote (use 3.14 for pi).
choices: 43.96 sq ft: that is the circumference (2 x 3.14 x 7).
22.0 sq ft: used diameter 7 as radius... actually used r = 3.5 incorrectly halved.
307.72 sq ft: used diameter 14 as the radius.
scenarios.why: The correct approach squares the radius first (49), then multiplies by pi: 153.86 sq ft. The 43.96 distractor is the circumference formula — the C/A swap. The 307.72 comes from squaring the diameter (14^2 = 196 x 3.14): when an answer is ~4x too big, radius/diameter confusion is the prime suspect.
scenarios.hint: Which is bigger — the radius or the diameter? Which did you square?

scenarios.title: The Ladder Check
scenarios.situation: Safety rules: a ladder's foot must be 9 ft from the wall for a 12-ft reach up the wall.
choices: 15 ft: sqrt(9^2 + 12^2) = sqrt(81 + 144) = sqrt(225) = 15 — the 3-4-5 triple scaled by 3.
10.8 ft: arithmetic slip in the squares.
scenarios.why: The correct approach sees the right triangle: ground distance and wall height are legs, the ladder is the hypotenuse. sqrt(81 + 144) = sqrt(225) = 15. Recognizing 9-12-15 as 3x the 3-4-5 triple gives the answer without a calculator — triples are worth memorizing precisely for this.
scenarios.hint: Which sides are the legs, and which is the hypotenuse?
evidence: 9 ft out from wall, 12 ft up; ladder = hypotenuse

scenarios.title: The Storage Cubes
scenarios.situation: A storage box holds 120 cubic feet. You are packing 2-ft cubes (each 2x2x2 ft).
scenarios.prompt: How many cubes fit in the box?
scenarios.why: The correct approach computes the unit volume first: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 cubic feet per cube, then divides container by unit: 120/8 = 15. Packing problems always divide volumes — the distractors come from wrong unit volumes (2, 4, 6 instead of 8). Cubes pack without waste, so the division is exact.
scenarios.hint: What is the volume of ONE cube?

scenarios.title: The Sail Area
scenarios.situation: A triangular sail has base 14 ft and perpendicular height 9 ft.
choices: 46 sq ft: subtracted instead of multiplying.
scenarios.why: The correct approach applies the triangle formula with the perpendicular height: 1/2 x 14 x 9 = 7 x 9 = 63 sq ft. Forgetting the half is the dominant error (126). Note 'perpendicular height' is stated because the slanted edge would be longer — using it as height overstates the area.
scenarios.hint: Why does the problem say 'perpendicular' height?

scenarios.title: The Track Lane
scenarios.situation: A circular running track has diameter 14 m (use 3.14 for pi).
scenarios.prompt: What is the distance of one lap?
choices: 153.86 m: that is the area — wrong quantity for a lap.
43.96 m: C = pi x d = 3.14 x 14 = 43.96 — diameter given, so pi x d directly.
21.98 m: halved it (used radius 7 in pi x d as pi x r... actually 3.14 x 7).
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches given-to-formula: diameter is given, so C = pi x d = 43.96 m with no conversion needed. The 153.86 distractor is the area (pi x 7^2) — quantity mismatch again. When the diameter is handed to you, pi x d is the one-step path; converting to radius first just adds error surface.
scenarios.hint: You are given the diameter — which circumference formula uses it directly?

scenarios.title: The Map Distance
scenarios.situation: On a grid map, the warehouse is at (0, 0) and the depot at (3, 4) (units: km).
choices: 7 km: added the differences without squaring.
25 km: forgot the final square root.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recognizes Pythagoras on the grid: legs 3 and 4, hypotenuse 5 — the 3-4-5 triple again. Distance is the straight-line hypotenuse, not the walked path (7) or the squared distance (25). Grid problems are triangle problems wearing coordinates.
scenarios.hint: What are the horizontal and vertical differences? What triangle do they make?

domains.name: Statistics for Operations

scenarios.title: The Daily Average
scenarios.situation: Five days of sales: $12k, $15k, $18k, $21k, $14k. Your manager asks for the average daily sales.
choices: $15k: that is the median, not the mean.
$18k: the middle of the range, not the mean.
$14k: the most recent day, not the average.
scenarios.why: The correct approach sums all five days (80) and divides by 5: $16k. The $15k distractor is the median — a fine 'typical day' number, but the question asked for the mean. Naming which average you computed matters as much as computing it.
scenarios.hint: What does 'mean' require you to do with all five numbers?

scenarios.title: The Typical Ticket Time
scenarios.situation: Resolution times (hours): 5, 8, 8, 12, 20, 8, 3. You want the 'typical' time for the team dashboard.
scenarios.prompt: Which measure is most appropriate, and what is it?
choices: Mean = 9.14 hours: the 20-hour case drags it above typical.
Median = 8 hours: sort to 3, 5, 8, 8, 8, 12, 20; the middle is 8 — resistant to the 20-hour outlier.
Mode = 20: 20 appears once; the mode is 8.
scenarios.why: The correct approach sorts first (3, 5, 8, 8, 8, 12, 20) and takes the middle: 8. The mean (64/7 = 9.14) is pulled up by the single 20-hour ticket, overstating 'typical'. For a dashboard describing normal experience, the median's outlier resistance is exactly the property you want.
scenarios.hint: Sort the data. Where is the middle? What pulls the mean away?

scenarios.title: The Temperature Swing
scenarios.situation: High temperatures for the week: 45, 52, 38, 61, 47 (F). Facilities asks how much temperatures varied.
choices: 47 F: the median, not the spread.
scenarios.why: The correct approach takes max minus min: 61 - 38 = 23 F. The 15 distractor drops the 61 — but the range is defined by the extremes, outliers included; you note the outlier, you do not quietly exclude it. Range answers the 'how much did it vary' question directly.
scenarios.hint: What are the highest and lowest values?

scenarios.title: The Final Grade
scenarios.situation: Midterm 70 (40% of grade), final 90 (60% of grade). What is the course grade?
scenarios.prompt: What is the weighted course grade?
choices: 80: the unweighted mean — ignores the stated weights.
scenarios.why: The correct approach multiplies each score by its weight and sums: 28 + 54 = 82. The unweighted 80 treats both exams equally, contradicting the problem. Weight-direction errors (78) are caught by asking 'which exam counts more?' before computing.
scenarios.hint: Which exam counts more? Does your math reflect that?

scenarios.title: The New Data Point
scenarios.situation: Three machines average 10 units/hour (6, 10, 14). A fourth machine producing 30 units/hour joins the line.
choices: 12: averaged the old mean with the new value (10+30)/2 — wrong, unequal counts.
10: assumed the average cannot move that much.
scenarios.why: The correct approach returns to totals: the old total was 3 x 10 = 30, plus 30 = 60, divided by 4 = 15. Averaging the averages ((10+30)/2 = 20... the 12 distractor uses yet another wrong blend) fails because the groups have different sizes. Totals never lie — recompute from them.
scenarios.hint: What was the old total? Add the new machine, then divide by what?
evidence: 3 machines at 6, 10, 14 u/h; add one at 30 u/h

scenarios.title: The Salary Survey
scenarios.situation: Five salaries (thousands): 10, 11, 12, 13, 54. HR wants one number for 'typical pay'.
choices: Median 12k as typical, with the mean 20k flagged as outlier-driven: honest reporting shows both and names the distortion.
54k: the max is the most informative.
scenarios.why: The correct approach refuses the single misleading number: the mean ($20k) describes nobody — four people earn ~11-13k. Report the median ($12k) as typical and disclose the mean with its cause ('one $54k value lifts the mean to $20k'). Silent deletion is dishonest; the max alone is not 'typical'.
scenarios.hint: Which number describes four of the five people?

scenarios.title: The Missing Value
scenarios.situation: Four measurements average 15. Three are known: 8, 12, 20. What is the fourth?
scenarios.prompt: What is the missing fourth value?
choices: 15: assumed the missing value equals the mean.
12: the median of the known three.
scenarios.why: The correct approach works backward from the total: mean 15 over 4 values means the sum is 60. Known values sum to 40, so the missing value is 20. 'Equals the mean' is a guess that happens to fail here — the total is the constraint, not the average.
scenarios.hint: If the average is 15, what must the four numbers add up to?

domains.description: Mean, median, mode, range, and weighted averages — summarizing data honestly.

domains.name: Probability Basics

scenarios.title: The Marble Bag
scenarios.situation: A bag holds 5 red, 3 blue, 2 green marbles, well mixed. You draw one without looking.
choices: 5/3: compared red to blue instead of to total.
scenarios.why: The correct approach counts favorable over total: 5 red / 10 marbles = 1/2, simplified. The 5/3 error compares red to blue (a ratio, not a probability); 1/5 counts categories instead of outcomes. Probability's denominator is always total possible outcomes.
scenarios.hint: How many marbles total? How many are red?

scenarios.title: The Die Roll
scenarios.situation: You roll a fair six-sided die. You win unless it shows 6.
choices: 1/6: that is P(6) — the complement of what was asked.
5/5: nonsense fraction above... equals 1, impossible here.
scenarios.why: The correct approach uses the complement: 1 - 1/6 = 5/6. Five winning faces out of six. The 1/6 distractor answers the unasked question — under pressure, 'not' gets skipped in reading, so circle the word 'not' before computing.
scenarios.hint: How many faces win? Out of how many?
evidence: fair d6; win on anything but 6

scenarios.title: The Two Coins
scenarios.situation: You flip two fair coins. You need both heads to win the toss.
choices: 1/3: counted HH, HT, TH as three outcomes (missed TT).
3/4: that is P(at least one head).
scenarios.why: The correct approach multiplies independent probabilities: 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4. The 1/3 error comes from listing three 'types' (HH, HT/TH, TT) as if equally likely — they are not (HT and TH are distinct). Four equally likely outcomes, one favorable: 1/4.
scenarios.hint: List all four outcomes. How many are HH?

scenarios.title: The Spinner
scenarios.situation: A spinner has 8 equal sections; 3 are marked WIN. You spin once.
scenarios.prompt: What is P(WIN), as a percent?
scenarios.why: The correct approach computes 3/8 = 0.375, then moves the decimal two places: 37.5%. Equal sections license the counting method. The 8/3 inversion gives 266% — probabilities over 100% are the instant signal to recheck which number is on top.
scenarios.hint: Favorable over total: which is which? Then convert.

scenarios.title: The Carnival Game
scenarios.situation: A game costs $2 to play. You win $10 with probability 1/4, otherwise nothing.
scenarios.prompt: What is the expected value per play?
choices: +$0.50: EV = (10 x 1/4) - 2 = 2.50 - 2 = 0.50. Positive — favors the player long-run.
-$2.00: assumed a loss (it is positive EV).
scenarios.why: The correct approach nets expected winnings against cost: 10 x 0.25 = $2.50 expected win, minus $2 cost = +$0.50. Positive EV means playing repeatedly profits on average — but 75% of single plays lose, so EV is a strategy for the long run, not a promise for tonight.
scenarios.hint: What do you expect to win per play? What does it cost?

scenarios.title: The Card Draw
scenarios.situation: From a standard 52-card deck, you draw one card.
choices: 1/52: counted one ace instead of four.
scenarios.why: The correct approach counts 4 aces over 52 cards and simplifies: 4/52 = 1/13. Simplification matters — 4/52 unsimplified will not match the answer choices, and 1/13 is instantly comparable to other probabilities.
scenarios.hint: How many aces in a deck? Simplify the fraction.

scenarios.title: The Two Draws
scenarios.situation: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue marbles. You draw two WITHOUT replacement.
choices: 5/14: 5/8 x 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14 — the bag shrinks after the first draw.
5/8: that is only the first draw.
scenarios.why: The correct approach adjusts for the changed bag: after drawing one red, 4 reds remain of 7 marbles, so 5/8 x 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14. The 25/64 distractor uses with-replacement math — the defining question is always 'did the first draw change the setup?' Without replacement, it did.
scenarios.hint: After the first red draw, how many marbles remain? How many red?

domains.description: Chance, complements, compound events, and expected value — reasoning under uncertainty.

domains.name: Financial Math

scenarios.title: The Loan Interest
scenarios.situation: You borrow $2,500 at 6% simple annual interest for 4 years. How much interest will you pay?
choices: $3,100: that is principal + interest (the total, not the interest).
scenarios.why: The correct approach applies I = Prt with the rate as a decimal: 2500 x 0.06 x 4 = $600. The $3,100 distractor answers 'total owed' — read whether the question asks for interest or total. The $150 is a single year's slice; the rate must be 0.06, not 6.
scenarios.hint: What is 6% as a decimal? What does I = Prt give?

scenarios.title: The Savings Growth
scenarios.situation: You deposit $5,000 at 4% compounded annually for 2 years. What is the account worth?
scenarios.prompt: What is the final account value?
scenarios.why: The correct approach compounds: 1.04^2 = 1.0816, times 5,000 = $5,408. Simple interest gives $5,400 — the $8 gap is interest-on-interest, small here but enormous over decades. Computing (1.04)^2 as 1.08 (instead of 1.0816) is the rounding trap.
scenarios.hint: What is 1.04 squared — exactly?

scenarios.title: The Sale Price
scenarios.situation: A $120 tool is 30% off. What do you pay?
choices: $36: that is the discount amount, not the price.
scenarios.why: The correct approach multiplies by the complement: (1 - 0.30) = 0.70, so 120 x 0.70 = $84 — one step instead of compute-then-subtract. The $36 distractor is the discount itself; the question asks what you PAY. Percent-off means dollars-off only when the price is $100.
scenarios.hint: If 30% comes off, what fraction remains?

scenarios.title: The Better Buy
scenarios.situation: Paper towels: 12-pack for $8.40 vs 8-pack for $6.00. Which is the better buy?
scenarios.prompt: Which option has the lower unit price?
choices: The 8-pack: lower sticker price, higher unit price.
They are equal: 8.40/12 vs 6.00/8 only look different.
Cannot tell without the roll size.
The 12-pack: $8.40/12 = $0.70 per roll vs $6.00/8 = $0.75 — the 12-pack saves $0.05/roll.
scenarios.why: The correct approach reduces both to unit price: $0.70 vs $0.75 per roll. Sticker price misleads — the 8-pack 'feels' cheaper at $6.00 but costs more per roll. Unit pricing is the universal solvent for package-size confusion; always divide before deciding.
scenarios.hint: What does each option cost per roll?

scenarios.title: The Savings Target
scenarios.situation: You earn $3,200/month and commit to saving 15% off the top. How much is saved monthly?
scenarios.prompt: What is the monthly savings amount?
choices: $2,720: that is what remains after saving.
scenarios.why: The correct approach converts 15% to 0.15 and multiplies: $480, transferred on payday before spending. The $2,720 distractor is the remainder — the question asks what is SAVED. Pay-yourself-first only works if the savings move before the spending happens.
scenarios.hint: What is 10% of $3,200? What is half of that (5%)? Add them.

scenarios.title: The Markup
scenarios.situation: A shop buys a part for $40 and marks it up 25%. What is the selling price?
scenarios.why: The correct approach multiplies by (1 + rate): 40 x 1.25 = $50. Markup is on COST — 25% of $40 is $10, added to $40. The $65 error treats 25 as dollars; the margin/markup distinction (margin is on price) matters in business but the math here is cost-based.
scenarios.hint: What is 25% of $40? Add it to the cost.

scenarios.title: Simple vs Compound
scenarios.situation: $1,000 at 10% for 2 years: how much MORE interest does compounding pay versus simple?
choices: $0: they are the same for 2 years.
$110: that is the second year's compound interest alone.
$1,210: that is the compound total, not the difference.
scenarios.why: The correct approach computes both: compound interest = 1000(1.21 - 1) = $210; simple = 1000 x 0.10 x 2 = $200. The $10 difference is interest-on-interest — tiny at 2 years, transformative at 20. Reading 'how much more' as 'compute the difference' defeats the total-value distractors.
scenarios.hint: Compute each interest amount first. Then subtract.

domains.description: Simple and compound interest, discounts, markups, unit pricing, and budgeting.

domains.name: Measurement & Conversion

scenarios.title: The Marathon Distance
scenarios.situation: A marathon is 26.2 miles. A European friend asks how far that is in kilometers (1 mile = 1.609 km).
scenarios.prompt: What is the distance in kilometers?
choices: 68.1 km: multiplied by 2.6 (km per... something else).
26.2 km: kept the number, changed the unit.
scenarios.why: The correct approach multiplies by the bridge: 26.2 x 1.609 = 42.16 km. Direction check: kilometers are smaller than miles, so the number must get BIGGER (42 > 26) — the 16.3 distractor fails this check instantly. Unit-labeling (km/mi) confirms the setup.
scenarios.hint: Should the kilometer number be bigger or smaller than 26.2?

scenarios.title: The Luggage Limit
scenarios.situation: The airline allows 2.5 kg of extra carry-on... actually your bag weighs 2.5 kg over and the fee chart is in pounds (1 kg = 2.205 lb).
scenarios.prompt: How many pounds overweight are you?
choices: 2.5 lb: kept the number, changed the unit.
scenarios.why: The correct approach multiplies: 2.5 x 2.205 = 5.5125 ≈ 5.5 lb. Kilograms are bigger units than pounds, so the pound number must be bigger than 2.5 — direction check kills the 1.13 distractor. Rounding 2.205 to 2.2 for a quick estimate (5.5) cross-checks the exact math.
scenarios.hint: Are pounds bigger or smaller than kilograms? Which way does the number go?

scenarios.title: The Shift Length
scenarios.situation: Your shift runs 9:45 AM to 2:20 PM. How long is that for the timesheet?
choices: 5 hours 35 minutes: forgot the AM/PM conversion on 2:20.
4 hours 25 minutes: borrowing slip in the minutes.
7 hours 25 minutes: added instead of subtracting.
scenarios.why: The correct approach converts to minutes-since-midnight (585 and 860), subtracts (275 min), and converts back: 4h 35m. Direct clock subtraction invites borrowing errors; the minutes method is one clean subtraction. Sanity: 9:45 AM to 2:20 PM is clearly under 5 hours, killing the 5h35m and 7h25m options.
scenarios.hint: Convert both times to minutes after midnight, then subtract.

scenarios.title: The Thermostat
scenarios.situation: The thermostat reads 72 F. Your recipe (European) needs the kitchen at about 22 C. Is 72 F close?
choices: 161.6 F... 161.6 C: forgot to subtract 32 first (72 x 5/9 = 40... actually 72 x 9/5 = 129.6 + 32). Way off.
20 C: close estimate but not exact.
scenarios.why: The correct approach subtracts 32 first (the offset), then scales: (72-32) = 40, x 5/9 = 22.2 C. Anchor check: 68 F = 20 C (room temp), so 72 F slightly warmer at 22.2 C is exactly right. Forgetting the 32 gives absurd answers — the anchor catches them.
scenarios.hint: What must come off before the 5/9 scaling?

scenarios.title: The Fuel Can
scenarios.situation: You need 3 gallons of fuel for the generator. The station across town sells by the liter (1 gal = 3.785 L).
scenarios.prompt: How many liters do you buy?
scenarios.why: The correct approach multiplies: 3 x 3.785 = 11.355 ≈ 11.4 L. Liters are smaller than gallons, so the number grows (11.4 > 3) — direction check eliminates 7.9 and 0.79. The 11,355 distractor is a decimal catastrophe; estimating 'about 4 L per gallon, so about 12' rules it out before computing.
scenarios.hint: Should the liter number be bigger or smaller than 3?

scenarios.title: The Carpet Order
scenarios.situation: A room is 12 ft by 15 ft. Carpet is priced per square yard. How many square yards?
scenarios.prompt: How many square yards of carpet?
choices: 180 sq yd: forgot to convert — ordered 9x too much.
60 sq yd: divided by 3 (linear factor trap).
scenarios.why: The correct approach computes square feet first (180), then divides by 9 — the SQUARED linear factor (3^2). The 60 distractor used the linear 3: when an area conversion is 3x off, that is the tell. Square yards are bigger units, so the count (20) is smaller than square feet (180) — direction confirmed.
scenarios.hint: Is a square yard bigger or smaller than a square foot? By what factor?
objectives: Convert sq ft to sq yd
evidence: 12 ft x 15 ft; carpet by sq yd

scenarios.title: The Recipe Conversion
scenarios.situation: A recipe calls for 2.5 cups of milk. Your measuring jug is in milliliters (1 cup = 236.6 mL).
scenarios.why: The correct approach multiplies by the bridge: 2.5 x 236.6 = 591.5 ≈ 592 mL. Estimate check: about 240 mL per cup, 2.5 cups ≈ 600 mL — the answer must sit near 600, which only 592 does. Unit labeling (mL/cup) confirms cups cancel properly.
scenarios.hint: Roughly how many mL per cup? What must 2.5 cups be near?

domains.description: Length, weight, volume, time, temperature, and area conversions — the math of the physical world.

domains.name: Word Problems

scenarios.title: The Mystery Number
scenarios.situation: A client says: 'Twice a number, plus 7, is 31.' You need the number for the invoice calc.
scenarios.why: The correct approach translates mechanically: 'twice a number' = 2n, 'plus 7' = +7, 'is' = =, giving 2n + 7 = 31. Undo in reverse: subtract 7 (2n = 24), divide by 2 (n = 12). Check: 2(12) + 7 = 31. Each distractor is one specific undo error.
scenarios.hint: What does 'is' mean? What was done to n last?

scenarios.title: The Delivery Run
scenarios.situation: A driver averages 60 mph for 3.5 hours. Dispatch needs the distance covered.
scenarios.prompt: How far did the driver go?
choices: 180 miles: used 3 hours, dropped the half hour.
scenarios.why: The correct approach uses distance = rate x time: 60 x 3.5 = 210 miles. Units confirm: (miles/hour) x hours = miles. The 3.5 splits cleanly (3 x 60 = 180, 0.5 x 60 = 30) for exact mental math. Division would give miles-per-hour-per-hour — nonsense units, nonsense answer.
scenarios.hint: What are the units of rate x time?

scenarios.title: The Two-Person Job
scenarios.situation: Worker A finishes a job alone in 6 hours; worker B in 3 hours. Working together, how long?
scenarios.prompt: How long does the job take together?
scenarios.why: The correct approach converts times to rates (1/6 and 1/3 job per hour), adds the rates (1/2), and inverts back to time (2h). Sanity: together must beat the fastest alone (2 < 3) — confirmed. Adding or averaging times is the folk error; rates are what add.
scenarios.hint: Working together, should it take more or less than 3 hours?

scenarios.title: The Fenced Lot
scenarios.situation: A rectangular lot's length is 5 ft more than its width. The perimeter is 38 ft. Find the length.
choices: 7 ft: that is the width — answers the wrong question.
scenarios.why: The correct approach defines w, writes l = w + 5, and perimeters: 2(w + w + 5) = 38, so 4w = 28, w = 7, l = 12. Check: 2(7 + 12) = 38. The 7 distractor punishes not re-reading the question — the work finds width first, but 'length' was asked.
scenarios.hint: What did you solve for first — and what was asked?

scenarios.title: The Coffee Blend
scenarios.situation: Blend 10 lb of coffee at $5.50/lb from $4/lb and $7/lb beans. How much of the $4 beans?
scenarios.prompt: How many pounds of the $4 beans?
choices: 3 lb: setup error on the total value.
7 lb: solved for the wrong bean.
scenarios.why: The correct approach uses (10 - x) for the second bean, keeping one variable: 4x + 70 - 7x = 55, so 3x = 15, x = 5 lb. Reasonableness: $5.50 is midway between $4 and $7, so a 5/5 split is exactly expected — the math and the intuition agree.
scenarios.hint: If x lb is $4 beans, how much is $7 beans? What is the total value?

scenarios.title: The Consecutive Sum
scenarios.situation: Three consecutive integers sum to 87. What is the largest?
choices: 29: the middle one — not what was asked.
scenarios.why: The correct approach uses one variable in three forms (n, n+1, n+2): 3n + 3 = 87, n = 28, so the integers are 28, 29, 30 and the largest is 30. Check: 28 + 29 + 30 = 87. The distractors punish answering with n or n+1 instead of re-reading for 'largest'.
scenarios.hint: If n is the smallest, what are the other two? Which was asked for?

scenarios.title: The Ages
scenarios.situation: Maria is 3 times as old as her son. In 5 years, she will be twice as old as he will be. How old is Maria now?
choices: 15: let s = son now; 3s + 5 = 2(s + 5) -> s = 5; Maria = 3 x 5 = 15.
scenarios.why: The correct approach anchors on now: son = s, Maria = 3s. In 5 years BOTH age: 3s + 5 = 2(s + 5), giving s = 5 and Maria = 15. Check: now 15 and 5 (3x); in 5 years 20 and 10 (2x). Adding 5 to only one side is the classic setup break.
scenarios.hint: In 5 years, how old is each person in terms of s?
evidence: Maria = 3 x son now; in 5 years Maria = 2 x son

domains.description: Translating English into equations: the most-tested applied skill in operations math.

domains.name: Data Interpretation

scenarios.title: The Weekly Total
scenarios.situation: Daily sales ($k): Mon 120, Tue 150, Wed 90, Thu 180, Fri 200. The regional manager wants the week's total.
scenarios.why: The correct approach sums the labeled values: 120 + 150 = 270, + 90 = 360, + 180 = 540, + 200 = 740 ($k). Group for mental math: (120 + 180) + (150 + 90 + 200)... verify by re-adding in a different order. Bar charts give exact numbers only through their labels.
scenarios.hint: Add the five labeled values. Then re-add in a different order to verify.

scenarios.title: The Morning Warmup
scenarios.situation: A temperature line graph shows 58 F at 6 AM and 76 F at noon.
scenarios.prompt: How much did it warm up?
choices: 76 F: read the endpoint, not the change.
scenarios.why: The correct approach subtracts: change = later minus earlier = 76 - 58 = 18 F. Change is always a difference — the endpoint alone (76) answers a different question ('how warm was it?'). Rate bonus: 18 F over 6 hours = 3 F/hour.
scenarios.hint: Is 'how much did it change' asking for a value or a difference?

scenarios.title: The Survey Slice
scenarios.situation: A pie chart: 40% of 250 surveyed customers prefer option X.
choices: 62.5: divided by 4 instead of multiplying by 0.40.
scenarios.why: The correct approach converts 40% to 0.40 and multiplies by the total: 100 customers. Percents need their base — '40%' alone is not a count. The 40 distractor treats the percent sign as decoration; always ask '40% of WHAT?' first.
scenarios.hint: 40% of what? Convert and multiply.

scenarios.title: The Best Month
scenarios.situation: Monthly units sold: Jan 120, Feb 150, Mar 140, Apr 200, May 210. Which month had the greatest INCREASE over the previous month?
scenarios.prompt: Which month, and by how much?
choices: February, +30: second largest, not the max.
May, +10: small gain on a big base.
April, +60: changes are +30, -10, +60, +10 — April's +60 is largest.
scenarios.why: The correct approach computes each month-to-month difference first (+30, -10, +60, +10), then takes the max: April +60. 'Greatest increase' means max difference, not max value (May's 210 is the max value but only +10 growth). The distinction is the whole question.
scenarios.hint: Compute each month's change first. Then which is biggest?
objectives: Distinguish max value vs max increase

scenarios.title: The Suspicious Chart
scenarios.situation: A vendor's bar chart shows their product's bar towering ~3x over a competitor's. The y-axis starts at 48; values are 54 vs 50.
choices: An 8% difference (54/50 = 1.08) — the truncated axis exaggerates it ~3x visually. Read the numbers, not the ink.
A 3x advantage — the chart shows it clearly.
The chart is fine; axes always start somewhere.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recomputes from the labels: 54 vs 50 is an 8% edge, while the visual screams 3x. Truncated axes are the oldest chart trick — the defense is reading axis numbers and recomputing the claim yourself. 'Up 4 points' is honest; the visual is not.
scenarios.hint: What do the axis labels say — and what does the ink imply?

scenarios.title: The Two Stores
scenarios.situation: Store A quarterly sales: 120, 150, 180. Store B: 100, 140, 190. The owner asks which grew more.
scenarios.prompt: Which store grew more, and by how much?
scenarios.why: The correct approach compares changes, not endpoints: A +60, B +90. B started lower and finished higher — the growth story belongs to B. Comparing endpoints (180 vs 190) nearly ties them and misses the point; growth is a difference, and differences need computing per series first.
scenarios.hint: Compute each store's total change first. Then compare.

scenarios.title: The Quarterly Average
scenarios.situation: Quarterly revenue ($k): Q1 300, Q2 450, Q3 375, Q4 525. Finance wants the average quarter.
scenarios.prompt: What is the average quarterly revenue?
choices: $1,650k: reported the total, not the average.
scenarios.why: The correct approach sums (300 + 450 + 375 + 525 = 1650) and divides by 4: $412.5k. Showing the total as an intermediate makes the work checkable — anyone can verify 1650/4. The $1,650 distractor answers 'total', a different question; precision matters in which question you answer.
scenarios.hint: What is the total? Over how many quarters?

domains.description: Reading bar charts, line graphs, pie charts, and tables — extracting truth from visuals.

domains.name: Estimation & Reasonableness

scenarios.title: The Quick Quote
scenarios.situation: A client asks on the phone: roughly what is 48 units at $21 each?
scenarios.prompt: What is the best quick estimate?
choices: $1,000: 50 x 20 = 1,000 — rounds one up, one down; actual 1,008.
$960: rounded both down (40 x 24?) — no, this under-shoots.
scenarios.why: The correct approach rounds to compatible numbers with canceling errors: 48 -> 50 (up), 21 -> 20 (down), giving 1,000 vs the actual 1,008 — under 1% off, computed in seconds. Rounding both the same direction compounds the error; the up/down pairing is the technique.
scenarios.hint: Round 48 and 21 to friendly numbers — one up, one down. Multiply.

scenarios.title: The Mental Total
scenarios.situation: Three invoices: $297, $512, $188. You need the total before the spreadsheet loads.
choices: $997: that is exact — admirable but not the estimate asked for.
scenarios.why: The correct approach rounds each to the nearest hundred and adds: 1,000 vs actual 997 — 0.3% off. The estimate's job is speed and bracketing, not precision; it also guards the spreadsheet total when it arrives (if the sheet says $9,970, the estimate objects immediately).
scenarios.hint: Round each to the nearest hundred, then add.

scenarios.title: The Tip Estimate
scenarios.situation: Bill is $450 (team dinner). Roughly what is an 18% tip?
choices: $81: exact — correct but not an estimate.
scenarios.why: The correct approach rounds the percent to the friendly 20% and computes: $90 vs actual $81 — close enough to decide and to check the card machine later. Anchoring on 10% ($45) and doubling is the same move. The estimate exists to be fast and sane, not exact.
scenarios.hint: What is 10% of $450? Double it — what percent is that near?

scenarios.title: The Register Check
scenarios.situation: The register shows 6 items at $4.97 each totaling... you glance: is ~$30 right?
scenarios.prompt: What is the best estimate, and does ~$30 check out?
scenarios.why: The correct approach rounds $4.97 to $5 (one cent of error per item, six cents total) and multiplies: $30 vs $29.82. The estimate validates the register total instantly — a $300 or $3.00 total would fail against it. Rounding to the nearest dollar is the right coarseness for price checks.
scenarios.hint: Round the price to the nearest dollar first. Then multiply.

scenarios.title: The Calculator Lie
scenarios.situation: A coworker's calculator shows 12 x 15 = 1800. They are about to order based on it.
choices: Wrong — estimate 10 x 15 = 150, so the answer is near 150-180, not 1,800: a decimal/extra-zero slip. The true value is 180.
Correct — calculators do not make mistakes.
Order based on it; close enough.
scenarios.why: The correct approach trusts the estimate over the machine: 10 x 15 = 150 brackets the truth near 180, exposing 1,800 as a 10x error (probably typed 12 x 150). Calculators compute exactly what is typed — including typos. The estimate is the human's veto over machine output.
scenarios.hint: Roughly what should 12 x 15 be? Does 1,800 sit near that?

scenarios.title: The Division Shortcut
scenarios.situation: You need roughly 8,432 / 9 for a capacity plan. No calculator handy.
choices: 937: exact — right but not the estimate.
scenarios.why: The correct approach picks a nearby numerator divisible by 9: 8,100/9 = 900 vs actual 937 — 4% off, instant. Compatible numbers are chosen for clean division, not closeness alone: 8,400/9 is closer but does not divide cleanly, defeating the purpose.
scenarios.hint: What nearby number divides cleanly by 9?

scenarios.title: The Percent Shortcut
scenarios.situation: About 19% of 200 applicants will be interviewed. Roughly how many?
scenarios.why: The correct approach rounds 19% to the friendly 20% and computes: 40 vs actual 38. For headcount planning, 40 is the actionable number — 'about forty interviews to schedule'. The estimate drives the decision; the exact 38 refines it later if needed.
scenarios.hint: Round 19% to a friendly percent. What is that of 200?

scenarios.title: Capstone Planning
scenarios.situation: You are about to start the Operations Math Portfolio capstone. You have limited lab time and want maximum interview value.
scenarios.prompt: How do you scope the build?
choices: Write the plan first: phases with definitions of done, mapped to bootcamp domains. Start with the smallest working core, then layer on complexity. Document decisions as you go.
Start building immediately — planning wastes lab time.
Attempt the most impressive architecture possible to stand out.
Build whatever is easiest to finish quickly.
scenarios.why: The correct approach balances ambition with completion: a planned, phased build that finishes is worth more than an impressive unfinished one. Mapping phases to domains turns the capstone into applied review of the whole course.
scenarios.hint: What does the interviewer actually evaluate in a project?
objectives: Phase work with definitions of done
evidence: 20 hours of lab time available over two weeks

scenarios.title: The Budget Defense
scenarios.situation: Your portfolio budget allocates $2,720/month after 15% savings on $3,200 income. A reviewer asks: 'Why 15%, and what breaks if income drops 20%?'
choices: 15% is standard; the budget still works if income drops.

15% is the pay-yourself-first target that builds the emergency fund; a 20% income drop ($2,560) keeps savings at $384 and forces the 50/30/20 split to re-balance — show the recomputed table, not just the original.
Cut savings to zero if income drops — spending comes first.
The percentages do not matter as long as it adds up.
scenarios.why: The correct approach defends the number with its purpose (emergency fund velocity) and stress-tests it: recompute at $2,560 income — savings $384, remaining $2,176 re-split — showing the method survives shocks. A budget that cannot answer 'what if income drops?' is a spreadsheet, not a plan.

lessons.title: Operations Math - Core concepts
concepts: Knowledge checks sample your knowledge state with short, targeted questions - answer from understanding, show your setup, and treat wrong answers as a map of what to study next.
Dimensional analysis: carry units through every step and cancel them. Most operations math errors are unit errors wearing a disguise.
Rates and ratios run operations: throughput, utilization, SLA attainment. Always ask what the denominator is - '99% uptime' of what, measured how?
Schedule by working backwards: from the deadline, subtract lead times and handoffs to find the latest safe start. Buffers protect the plan; hope does not.
Inventory math: reorder point = demand during lead time + safety stock. Stockouts and overstocks are both failures - size for variability, not the average.
Estimate before you calculate: a 30-second Fermi bound catches order-of-magnitude mistakes that precise arithmetic will happily preserve.

example.code:
quoted_gb = 500                      # vendor decimal GB
gib = quoted_gb * 1000**3 / 1024**3  # what the system bills
print(f"{quoted_gb} GB (decimal) = {gib:.2f} GiB (binary)")
example.walkthrough: Vendors quote decimal gigabytes; systems bill binary gibibytes. The conversion shows 500 GB is only about 465.66 GiB - budget the shortfall before you sign, not after the first invoice.

pitfalls: Common trap: mixing GB and GiB in capacity plans - a 7% gap per unit compounds across petabytes.
Common trap: confusing percent change with absolute change - 50 to 75 is +25 absolute but a 50% increase; 'percentage points' only applies when the values themselves are percentages.
Common trap: averaging rates with the arithmetic mean - average speed over equal distances needs the harmonic mean.
Common trap: planning to the average - size buffers for variability (p95), not the mean.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Aleks Ops Math move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of Operations Math
concepts: Operations Math is a multi-step process within Operations Math: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect Operations Math to the broader Operations Math ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:
Step 1: Initiation
  Operations Math begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing
  Data flows through — what transforms it?

Step 3: Handoff
  Result passes to next system — what is the interface?

Step 4: Completion

example.walkthrough: Apply the four-step anatomy method to Operations Math. Draw it as a flowing sequence, not a static diagram.

pitfalls: Treating Operations Math as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists
