lessons.title: Order of Operations (PEMDAS)
concepts: PEMDAS is the agreed reading order for math: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication/Division (left to right), Addition/Subtraction (left to right)
Multiplication and division are equals — work them left to right, not 'all multiplication first': 12 / 3 * 2 = 8, not 2
Exponents bind tighter than multiplication: 4 x 2^2 = 16, because 2^2 = 4 is computed before the 4 x 4
When in doubt, add parentheses to your own work — explicit grouping beats implicit rules for preventing errors

example.code:
3 + 4 x 2^2 - 10 / 5
= 3 + 4 x 4 - 2      (exponent, then divide)
= 3 + 16 - 2         (multiply left to right)
= 17                 (add/subtract left to right)
example.walkthrough: Work inside-out by precedence: 2^2 becomes 4 and 10/5 becomes 2 first. Then multiplication: 4 x 4 = 16. Finally left to right: 3 + 16 = 19, minus 2 = 17. The classic error is computing 3 + 4 = 7 first (left-to-right reading) to get 7 x 4 - 2 = 26 — wrong, because addition waits its turn.

pitfalls: Reading strictly left to right — addition and subtraction go last, not first
Doing all multiplication before all division — they are the same level, left to right
Forgetting that a negative base needs parentheses: -3^2 = -9 but (-3)^2 = 9
lessons.try_it: Evaluate 8 + 6 / 2 x 3 - 4 step by step, showing each precedence level.

lessons.title: Fractions: Add, Subtract, Multiply, Divide
concepts: Adding/subtracting needs common denominators: convert first, then operate on numerators — 2/3 + 5/6 = 4/6 + 5/6 = 9/6 = 3/2
Multiplying is direct: multiply numerators, multiply denominators, then simplify — 3/4 x 8/9 = 24/36 = 2/3
Dividing means multiplying by the reciprocal (flip the second fraction): 5/6 / 2/3 = 5/6 x 3/2 = 15/12 = 5/4
'Of' means multiply: 5/8 of 96 = 5/8 x 96 = 60 — the fastest fraction skill on any assessment

example.walkthrough: Addition: only 2/3 needs converting (multiply top and bottom by 2 to get 4/6). Multiplication: cancel before multiplying when you can — 3/4 x 8/9: the 3 and 9 share 3, the 4 and 8 share 4, leaving 1/1 x 2/3 = 2/3 directly. Division: flip 2/3 to 3/2 and multiply. 'Of 96': divide 96 by 8 first (12), then times 5 — always divide before multiplying to keep numbers small.

pitfalls: Adding numerators and denominators separately: 1/2 + 1/3 is NOT 2/5
Forgetting to flip the second fraction when dividing
Skipping simplification — 24/36 unsimplified often will not match the answer choices
lessons.try_it: Compute 7/8 - 1/4 and 2/3 / 4/5, simplifying fully.

lessons.title: Decimals and Percents
concepts: Percent means 'per hundred': 35% = 35/100 = 0.35 — move the decimal two places to convert either direction
Finding a percent of a number: convert to decimal and multiply — 15% of 240 = 0.15 x 240 = 36
Percent change = (new - old) / old x 100%: from 80 to 100 is (20/80) x 100% = 25% increase
Benchmark percents for mental math: 10% (move decimal one place), then scale — 20% is double 10%, 5% is half

example.walkthrough: The 18% tip shows benchmark thinking: 10% of $50 is $5 (decimal shift), 5% is half of that ($2.50), 3% is roughly $1.50 — sum to $9.00 without a calculator. For percent change, the denominator is always the ORIGINAL value: 80 to 100 uses 80, not 100. Mixing that up is the most expensive percent error.

pitfalls: Using the new value as the denominator in percent change
Converting 0.35 to 3.5% — two decimal places, not one
Adding percents directly across different bases — 10% off then 10% on is not back to start
lessons.try_it: Compute: 12% of 350, and the percent decrease from 200 to 150.

lessons.title: Integers, Exponents, and Roots
concepts: Sign rules: negative x negative = positive; (-3)^2 = 9 but -3^2 = -9 (the exponent binds before the minus sign)
Exponent laws: multiply powers by adding exponents (2^3 x 2^2 = 2^5 = 32); anything to the zero power is 1
Square roots undo squares: sqrt(144) = 12 because 12^2 = 144 — memorize perfect squares through 15^2 = 225
Order matters with negatives: (-2)^3 = -8 (odd power keeps the sign), (-2)^4 = 16 (even power flips it positive)

example.code:
(-3)^2 = 9        (parentheses: negative squared)
-3^2 = -9          (exponent first, then negate)
2^3 x 2^2 = 2^5 = 32
sqrt(144) = 12    (12 x 12 = 144)
(-2)^3 + sqrt(81) - 4^2 = -8 + 9 - 16 = -15
example.walkthrough: The worked line combines everything: (-2)^3 = -8 (odd power, sign stays), sqrt(81) = 9, 4^2 = 16 — then -8 + 9 - 16 = -15 left to right. Notice -4^2 would be -16 while (-4)^2 is +16: the parentheses decide. These sign rules are where most assessment points leak away, so slow down on every negative base.

pitfalls: (-3)^2 vs -3^2 — the parentheses flip the sign of the answer
Adding exponents when multiplying powers with different bases — 2^3 x 3^2 is NOT 6^5
sqrt(a + b) = sqrt(a) + sqrt(b) — false; sqrt(9 + 16) = 5, not 7
lessons.try_it: Evaluate (-4)^2, -4^2, and (-2)^4, explaining each sign.

lessons.title: Solving One- and Two-Step Equations
concepts: The golden rule: do the same operation to both sides — the equation is a balanced scale, and balance is everything
Undo in reverse order of operations: for 3x + 7 = 25, subtract 7 first (undoes the +), then divide by 3 (undoes the x)
Always check by substitution: x = 6 gives 3(6) + 7 = 25 — 30 seconds that catches most errors
Fractions clear by multiplying everything by the common denominator — never wrestle fractions term by term

example.code:
3x + 7 = 25
3x = 25 - 7 = 18      (subtract 7 both sides)
x = 18 / 3 = 6          (divide by 3 both sides)
Check: 3(6) + 7 = 18 + 7 = 25  ✓
example.walkthrough: Reverse the order of operations: the +7 was applied last when building the expression, so it comes off first. Subtracting 7 from both sides keeps the scale balanced, leaving 3x = 18; dividing both sides by 3 isolates x = 6. The check substitutes back into the ORIGINAL equation — checking against your own algebra just re-confirms your mistake.

pitfalls: Subtracting 7 from only one side — the scale tips and the answer is fiction
Dividing before subtracting: 3x + 7 = 25 does not give x + 7 = 8.33
Skipping the check — substitution catches sign slips in seconds
lessons.try_it: Solve 5x - 9 = 31 and check by substitution.

lessons.title: Variables on Both Sides
concepts: Collect variables first: move all x terms to one side, all constants to the other — 5x - 9 = 2x + 12 becomes 3x = 21
Subtract the smaller variable term to keep the coefficient positive: subtract 2x (not 5x) to avoid negative-x arithmetic
Distribute before collecting: 2(x + 3) = 5x - 9 becomes 2x + 6 = 5x - 9, then collect
If the variables cancel and constants remain (3 = 7), there is no solution; if everything cancels (5 = 5), infinitely many

example.code:
2(x + 3) = 5x - 9
2x + 6 = 5x - 9        (distribute)
6 + 9 = 5x - 2x        (collect: constants left, x right)
15 = 3x  ->  x = 5
Check: 2(8) = 16; 5(5) - 9 = 16  ✓
example.walkthrough: Distribute first — 2(x + 3) is 2x + 6, not 2x + 3. Then collect: move 2x right (subtract from both sides) and -9 left (add to both sides), keeping x positive: 15 = 3x, so x = 5. The check evaluates both ORIGINAL sides independently: left 2(5+3) = 16, right 5(5)-9 = 16. Both 16 — solved.

pitfalls: Forgetting to distribute to every term inside the parentheses
Sign errors when moving terms — subtracting 2x from the left means -2x on the right
Checking against simplified work instead of the original equation
lessons.try_it: Solve 4(x - 2) = 3x + 5, showing the check.

lessons.title: Ratios and Proportions
concepts: A proportion sets two ratios equal: a/b = c/d — solve by cross-multiplying to ad = bc
Direct proportion: more workers, more output (multiply straight through); inverse: more workers, less time (flip one ratio)
Unit rates simplify comparisons: $8.40/12-pack vs $6.00/8-pack becomes $0.70 vs $0.75 per unit
Scale problems are proportions in disguise: 1 cm : 50 km on a map means 4 cm = 200 km

example.code:
3/5 = x/25  ->  5x = 75  ->  x = 15
12 workers -> 8 days; 16 workers -> ? days (inverse)
12 x 8 = 16 x d  ->  d = 96/16 = 6 days
example.walkthrough: Direct: cross-multiply 3/5 = x/25 to get 5x = 75, x = 15. Inverse (workers/days): more workers means fewer days, so the products are equal, not the ratios — 12 x 8 = 16 x d gives d = 6. The key judgment is direct vs inverse: ask 'does more of A mean more of B?' If yes, direct; if no, inverse with flipped setup.

pitfalls: Setting up inverse problems as direct — more workers, more days is nonsense
Cross-multiplying incorrectly: 3/5 = x/25 gives 5x = 75, not 3x = 125
Forgetting units — the answer 6 needs 'days' attached
lessons.try_it: Solve: 5 lbs of apples cost $7.50. What do 8 lbs cost?

lessons.title: Functions and Slope
concepts: Function notation f(x) = 2x - 3 means 'plug the input into the formula': f(5) = 2(5) - 3 = 7
Slope = rise/run = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1): the rate of change between two points — steepness with direction
Positive slope climbs left to right, negative falls, zero is flat, undefined is vertical (division by zero in run)
From slope and a point you can build the line: point-slope form y - y1 = m(x - x1)

example.walkthrough: Evaluating f(5) is substitution: replace every x with 5. Slope counts vertical change over horizontal change between the points: up 8, right 4, so 2 units up per 1 right. Point-slope form then builds the full line equation from one point and that slope. Slope is the single most-tested algebra concept because it is 'rate of change' everywhere — speed, cost per unit, growth.

pitfalls: (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1) with mismatched order — keep point 1 and point 2 consistent top and bottom
Reading slope as run/rise — it is rise over run
f(5) = 7 means the point (5, 7) is on the graph — connect notation to geometry
lessons.try_it: Find the slope between (1, 5) and (4, 17), then write the line equation.

lessons.title: Perimeter and Area: Rectangles and Triangles
concepts: Perimeter is the fence (add all sides); area is the carpet (cover the surface) — never confuse the two
Rectangle: P = 2(l + w), A = l x w — the two formulas you will use most in practical math
Triangle: A = 1/2 x base x height, where height is perpendicular to the base — not the slanted side
Units tell the story: perimeter in feet, area in square feet — if your area answer is in 'feet', something is wrong

example.code:
Rectangle 12 ft by 7 ft:
  P = 2(12 + 7) = 38 ft
  A = 12 x 7 = 84 sq ft
Triangle base 10, height 6:
  A = 1/2 x 10 x 6 = 30 sq ft
example.walkthrough: Perimeter walks the boundary: 12 + 7 + 12 + 7 = 38. Area fills the inside: 12 x 7 = 84 square feet. For the triangle, height must be perpendicular to the base — using the slanted edge as 'height' is the classic error. The unit check is free verification: an area in plain feet is always wrong.

pitfalls: Using the slanted side as triangle height
Reporting area in linear units — square units or it did not happen
P = 2l + 2w computed as 2(l x w) — addition, not multiplication
lessons.try_it: A 15-by-9 garden: fence length? Soil area? State units.

lessons.title: Circles: Circumference and Area
concepts: Radius (r) is center-to-edge; diameter (d) is across: d = 2r — know which one you are given
Circumference C = 2 x pi x r = pi x d: the distance around
Area A = pi x r^2: note it is r SQUARED — doubling the radius quadruples the area
Use 3.14 for pi on assessments unless told otherwise; keep one extra decimal until the final step

example.walkthrough: The r = 5 walkthrough shows the pattern: circumference scales with r, area with r^2. For r = 7: square first (49), then times pi (153.86). The r-squared trap: using diameter as radius (or forgetting to square) roughly quadruples or quarters your answer — when a circle answer looks 4x off, check r vs d first.

pitfalls: Plugging diameter into pi x r^2 — square the radius, not the diameter
C = pi x r^2 or A = 2 x pi x r — formula swap under pressure
Rounding pi to 3 too early — keep 3.14 through the work
lessons.try_it: A circular table has diameter 14: find circumference and area.

lessons.title: The Pythagorean Theorem
concepts: For right triangles only: a^2 + b^2 = c^2, where c is the hypotenuse (longest side, opposite the right angle)
Memorize the triples: 3-4-5, 6-8-10, 5-12-13 — assessments love them because the arithmetic comes out clean
Finding a leg: c^2 - a^2 = b^2, then square-root — subtract before rooting, not after
Verify the right angle first: the theorem is false for non-right triangles, and diagrams are not always to scale

example.code:
Legs 6 and 8:  c^2 = 36 + 64 = 100  ->  c = 10
Hyp 13, leg 5:  b^2 = 169 - 25 = 144  ->  b = 12
Ladder: 9 ft out, 12 ft up -> sqrt(81+144) = 15 ft ladder
example.walkthrough: Legs 6 and 8: square both (36, 64), add (100), root (10) — the doubled 3-4-5 triple. Finding a leg reverses it: subtract the known leg's square from the hypotenuse's square, then root. The ladder problem is Pythagoras in work clothes: ground distance and wall height are the legs, the ladder is the hypotenuse.

pitfalls: Applying it to non-right triangles
Forgetting the final square root — answering 100 instead of 10
Adding instead of subtracting when finding a leg
lessons.try_it: A 9-12 right triangle: hypotenuse? A 10-hypotenuse, 6-leg triangle: other leg?

lessons.title: Volume: Boxes and Cylinders
concepts: Volume is 3D: length x width x height for boxes — cubic units, always
Box: V = l x w x h. Cylinder: V = pi x r^2 x h — the circular base area extruded by height
Packing problems divide volumes: how many 2-ft cubes fit in a 120-ft^3 box? 120 / 8 = 15
Like area, the unit check is free: volume in ft^2 or plain ft is always wrong

example.code:
Box 4 x 5 x 6:  V = 120 cubic ft
Cylinder r=3, h=10:  V = 3.14 x 9 x 10 = 282.6 cubic units
Packing: 2-ft cube = 8 ft^3; 120/8 = 15 cubes fit
example.walkthrough: The cylinder is base area (pi x r^2 = 28.26) times height (10) = 282.6 — 'area of the base, extruded'. Packing divides the container volume by the item volume: each 2-ft cube occupies 8 cubic feet, so 120/8 = 15 fit (assuming they pack without wasted space, which cubes do). Volume answers in square units are the giveaway of a missed dimension.

pitfalls: Volume in square units — count your dimensions: three for volume
Using diameter as r in pi x r^2 x h
Forgetting packing divides volumes — trying to line up cubes one dimension at a time
lessons.try_it: A cylindrical tank r=2, h=5: volume? How many gallons at 7.5 gal/ft^3?

lessons.title: Mean, Median, Mode
concepts: Mean = sum / count: the balance point of the data — sensitive to every value including outliers
Median = the middle value when sorted: the typical value, resistant to outliers
Mode = the most frequent value: the popular choice — a dataset can have no mode or several
Report the trio together when it matters: mean 6 / median 7 / mode 7 tells a fuller story than any one alone

example.code:
Data: 4, 7, 9, 7, 3
Mean:   (4+7+9+7+3)/5 = 30/5 = 6
Median: sort -> 3, 4, 7, 7, 9 -> middle = 7
Mode:   7 appears twice -> 7
example.walkthrough: Sort first for the median — the middle of unsorted data is meaningless. Here the mean (6) sits below the median (7) because the 3 drags it down: that gap is the outlier's fingerprint. When mean and median disagree substantially, the data is skewed and the median usually describes 'typical' better.

pitfalls: Computing the median without sorting
Reporting the mean alone on skewed data — the outlier writes the headline
Forgetting a dataset can have two modes (bimodal) or none
lessons.try_it: For 12, 15, 18, 21, 14: compute mean, median, mode.

lessons.title: Range and Spread
concepts: Range = max - min: the simplest spread measure — how wide the data stretches
Two datasets can share a mean but differ wildly in spread: {10, 10, 10} vs {0, 10, 20} both average 10
Range is fragile: one outlier defines it entirely — note the outlier when you report range
In operations, spread often matters more than center: consistent delivery times beat a good average with wild swings

example.code:
Data: 45, 52, 38, 61, 47
Range = 61 - 38 = 23
Mean  = 243/5 = 48.6
Note: the 61 stretches the range; without it, range = 52-38 = 14
example.walkthrough: The range is 23, but removing the single high value (61) drops it to 14 — one point owns 40% of the spread. That sensitivity is both the range's weakness and its use: a sudden range expansion is the cheapest anomaly signal in operations data. Always ask what defines the max and min before trusting the range.

pitfalls: Treating equal means as equal datasets — spread is the hidden difference
Ignoring which points set the range
Using range as the only spread measure on large datasets
lessons.try_it: Two delivery teams both average 30 min: A ranges 25-35, B ranges 10-60. Which is more reliable? Why?

lessons.title: Reading Averages in Context
concepts: An average without context misleads: 'average response 4 minutes' hides whether that is 4:00 every time or 0:30 vs 7:30
Ask three questions of any average: average of what, over whom, over what period — each choice changes the number
Survivorship distorts: 'average customer satisfaction among respondents' excludes everyone too angry to respond
Compare like with like: this month vs last month needs the same definition, same population, same period

example.code:
'Our technicians average 12 tickets/day'
Ask: which technicians? (all, or only full-time?)
     over what period? (this week? this quarter?)
     mean or median? (one hero tech can lift a mean)
example.walkthrough: Each question can flip the story: including part-timers lowers the mean; a holiday week is not a normal week; a mean of 12 with a median of 9 reveals skew. Averages are claims — interrogate the claim before acting on it. In operations reviews, the person asking these three questions is the most valuable person in the room.

pitfalls: Accepting headline averages without the three questions
Comparing averages computed differently across periods
Letting survivorship bias pick the population
lessons.try_it: Take one average from your work and answer the three questions for it.

lessons.title: Weighted Averages
concepts: Weighted average = sum(value x weight) / sum(weights): used when some values count more than others
Grades are the classic case: a final worth 60% moves the average more than a quiz worth 10%
Weights must sum sensibly: percentages should total 100% — if they do not, something is off
Unweighted mean of group means is wrong when groups differ in size — weight by group size

example.code:
Midterm 70 (weight 40%) + Final 90 (weight 60%):
  70 x 0.40 = 28
  90 x 0.60 = 54
  Total = 82
Plain mean (70+90)/2 = 80 -- wrong, ignores weights
example.walkthrough: The plain mean (80) pretends both exams count equally; the weighted 82 respects the 40/60 split. The two-point gap is the cost of ignoring weights. Same trap at scale: averaging department means without weighting by headcount gives small teams the same voice as large ones — always weight by what 'counts more' means in context.

pitfalls: Averaging averages without weighting by group size
Weights that do not sum to 100% going unquestioned
Using plain mean where the problem states weights
lessons.try_it: Quiz 80 (20%), project 90 (30%), exam 85 (50%): final grade?

lessons.title: Outliers: Spot, Question, Handle
concepts: An outlier is a value far from the rest: spot by sorting or by the mean/median gap — big gap, suspect skew
Question before handling: is it an error (fix/remove), a real extreme (keep, report separately), or the story itself?
Never silently delete outliers to make numbers pretty — that is data fraud with extra steps
Report with and without: 'mean $52k ($48k excluding one $500k outlier)' is honest; either number alone is spin

example.code:
Salaries: 10, 11, 12, 13, 54 (thousands)
Mean = 100/5 = 20 -> '$20k average' (misleading!)
Median = 12 -> '$12k typical'
Honest report: median 12k; mean 20k driven by one 54k value
example.walkthrough: The mean says $20k, the median says $12k — the $54k value owns the headline. Neither deletion nor blind inclusion is right by default: report the median as typical, the mean with the outlier flagged, and let the decision-maker see both. The outlier might be the CEO's salary (real, keep) or a data-entry slip (fix) — context decides, not statistics.

pitfalls: Deleting outliers silently to improve the numbers
Reporting the mean alone when an outlier dominates it
Treating every outlier as an error — some are the most important data you have
lessons.try_it: In 8, 9, 8, 10, 9, 200: identify the outlier and write the honest two-number report.

lessons.title: Probability as a Fraction
concepts: Probability = favorable outcomes / total possible outcomes — always a number between 0 and 1
A fair die: P(rolling 4) = 1/6 — one favorable face out of six
Convert freely: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50% — fractions for exactness, percents for communication
equally likely' is doing heavy lifting: only use total-counting when outcomes are truly symmetric

example.code:
Bag: 5 red, 3 blue, 2 green (10 total)
P(red) = 5/10 = 1/2
P(blue) = 3/10 = 0.3 = 30%
P(green) = 2/10 = 1/5
example.walkthrough: Count favorable over total: 5 red of 10 marbles is 1/2. Simplify the fraction (5/10 to 1/2) — unsimplified probabilities hide comparisons. The bag works because each marble is equally likely to be drawn; a weighted bag would need a different method entirely.

pitfalls: Probabilities above 1 or below 0 — impossible, recheck the counting
Forgetting to simplify — 5/10 and 1/2 are the same, but only one matches the choices
Assuming equally likely when it is not — loaded dice break the fraction
lessons.try_it: A deck: P(heart)? P(face card)? Simplify both.

lessons.title: Complements: The Easy Way Around
concepts: P(not A) = 1 - P(A): when 'at least one' or 'not' appears, the complement is usually easier
Die: P(not rolling 6) = 1 - 1/6 = 5/6 — counting five faces directly works too, but complements scale
P(at least one head in 3 flips) = 1 - P(no heads) = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8 — the complement turns 7 cases into 1
Complements must partition cleanly: A and not-A cover everything with no overlap, or the subtraction lies

example.code:
P(rain) = 0.3  ->  P(no rain) = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7
3 coins, P(at least one head):
  P(no heads) = 1/2 x 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/8
  P(at least one) = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8
example.walkthrough: Directly counting 'at least one head' means enumerating 7 of 8 outcomes; the complement counts the single all-tails case and subtracts. Whenever a problem says 'at least one' or 'none', reach for the complement first — it converts the hard counting problem into the easy one.

pitfalls: Computing P(at least one) by direct enumeration — error-prone past 2 events
1 - P(A) when A and not-A overlap — complements need clean partitions
Forgetting the complement exists and grinding the hard direction
lessons.try_it: P(at least one 6 in 2 dice) via complement.

lessons.title: Compound Events: Multiply When Independent
concepts: Independent events do not affect each other: coin flips, dice rolls, separate draws with replacement
P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B) for independent events: two heads = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4
Without replacement, events are dependent: P(both red from 5R/3B) = 5/8 x 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14 — the second draw's total changed
'And' multiplies (both happen), 'or' adds for mutually exclusive outcomes — match the operation to the word

example.code:
Two fair coins: P(both heads) = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4
Bag 5R 3B, two draws, no replacement:
  P(R then R) = 5/8 x 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14
Spinner 3 win / 8 total: P(win) = 3/8 = 37.5%
example.walkthrough: Independence is the license to multiply: coin flips qualify, sequential draws without replacement do not — the bag shrinks from 8 to 7 and reds from 5 to 4. The classic error multiplies 5/8 x 5/8 (as if replaced). Always ask: 'did the first outcome change the setup for the second?'

pitfalls: Multiplying without checking independence — the most-tested probability trap
'Or' treated as multiply — 'or' adds (for exclusive outcomes)
Using with-replacement math on without-replacement draws
lessons.try_it: Bag 4W 6B: P(white then black), no replacement.

lessons.title: Expected Value: Probability Meets Money
concepts: Expected value = sum(outcome x probability): the long-run average per play — the fair price of a gamble
EV guides decisions, not fortunes: positive EV is worth taking repeatedly; one play can still lose
Compute as: (win amount x P(win)) - cost, summed over all outcomes
Business EV works the same: expected profit = sum(scenario profit x scenario probability)

example.code:
Game: pay $2, win $10 with P = 1/4
EV = (10 x 1/4) - 2 = 2.50 - 2 = $0.50
Positive EV: worth playing repeatedly
(One play still loses 75% of the time!)
example.walkthrough: Each play averages a $0.50 profit over many plays: $2.50 in expected winnings minus the $2 cost. Positive EV means the game favors the player long-term — but 75% of individual plays lose, which is why EV is a strategy for repetition, not a prediction for tonight. Casinos live on this gap between expectation and experience.

pitfalls: Playing once because EV is positive — EV promises the average, not the outcome
Ignoring the cost term — EV nets winnings against price
Confusing 'most likely outcome' with expected value
lessons.try_it: Raffle: $5 ticket, 1/200 chance at $800. Compute EV. Buy?

lessons.title: Interpreting Risk Statements
concepts: '1 in 4 chance' = 25% = 0.25 — translate words to numbers before deciding anything
Relative vs absolute risk: 'double the risk' from 1% to 2% is +1 point, not +100 points — the base rate decides the meaning
Small probabilities compound over many trials: 1% per day over 100 days is ~63% at least once, not 100%
In operations, convert probabilities to expected counts: 2% failure over 500 units = ~10 expected failures — plan for 10

example.code:
'Double the risk' of a 1% defect rate:
  relative: 2x (sounds huge)
  absolute: 1% -> 2% (+1 point)
Expected failures: 500 units x 0.02 = 10 units
Plan spares for ~10, not ~0 and not ~500
example.walkthrough: The doubling sounds alarming until the absolute change (+1 point) puts it in perspective — always ask for the base rate. Expected counts turn abstract probabilities into concrete plans: 10 spare units, not panic and not complacency. This translation (probability -> expected count -> plan) is the operational skill.

pitfalls: Reacting to relative risk without the base rate
Adding small per-trial probabilities across trials (1% x 100 days != 100%)
Treating expected counts as guarantees — 10 expected means roughly 10, not exactly
lessons.try_it: A 0.5% defect rate on 2,000 units: expected defects? Spares to stock?

lessons.title: Simple Interest
concepts: Simple interest = Principal x rate x time: interest on the original amount only, same every period
Rate and time must match units: 6% annual for 4 years uses 0.06 and 4 — monthly rates need monthly time
Total owed = principal + interest: $2,500 at 6% for 4 years accrues $600 interest, $3,100 total
Solving for time or rate: rearrange I = Prt — t = I/(Pr) when the interest is known

example.walkthrough: Convert 6% to 0.06, multiply by principal and years: $600 of interest, linear in time. Simple interest never compounds — year 4 earns the same $150 as year 1. Assessments test whether you can rearrange too: given $600 interest on $2,500 at 6%, time = 600/(2500 x 0.06) = 4 years.

pitfalls: Using 6 instead of 0.06 — the percent-to-decimal conversion
Mixing monthly rate with yearly time
Reporting interest as the total (forgetting to add principal, or adding when asked for interest only)
lessons.try_it: Find the interest on $1,200 at 4.5% for 5 years; then the total.

lessons.title: Compound Interest
concepts: Compound interest earns interest on interest: A = P(1 + r)^t — growth accelerates each period
The compounding frequency matters: monthly compounding at 12%/12 per month beats annual at 12% — more periods, more growth
Rule of 72: years to double ~ 72 / rate%: at 6%, money doubles in ~12 years — the fastest mental estimate in finance

example.code:
$5,000 at 4% compounded annually, 2 years:
  A = 5000 x 1.04^2 = 5000 x 1.0816 = $5,408
  Interest = 5408 - 5000 = $408
Rule of 72: 72/4 = 18 years to double at 4%
example.walkthrough: Square 1.04 (1.0816), multiply by 5,000: $5,408 total, $408 of it interest. Compare simple ($400) — compounding added $8 in two years; over decades the gap becomes enormous. The Rule of 72 cross-checks: at 4%, doubling takes ~18 years, so 2 years should grow ~8% — and 5,408/5,000 = 1.0816 confirms it.

pitfalls: Computing (1+r)^t as 1 + r x t — that is simple interest wearing a costume
Forgetting to subtract principal when asked for interest (vs total)
Applying the annual rate per compounding period without dividing
lessons.try_it: $2,000 at 3% compounded annually for 3 years: total? Interest?

lessons.title: Discounts and Markups
concepts: Discount: sale price = original x (1 - rate): 30% off $120 = 120 x 0.70 = $84
Markup: price = cost x (1 + rate): $40 cost with 25% markup = 40 x 1.25 = $50
Successive discounts multiply, not add: 20% then 10% off = 0.80 x 0.90 = 0.72 (28% off total, not 30%)
Finding the original: original = sale / (1 - rate) — $84 after 30% off means 84/0.70 = $120 original

example.walkthrough: The (1 - rate) multiplier is the whole technique: one multiplication instead of compute-then-subtract. Successive discounts surprise people — 20% + 10% feels like 30% off but is 28%, because the second discount applies to the already-reduced price. Reverse problems divide by (1 - rate): the sale price is 70% of original, so original = sale/0.70.

pitfalls: Adding successive discount percents — multiply the complements instead
Discounting the discount: 30% off $120 is not $120 - $30
Markup on price instead of cost — margin vs markup confusion
lessons.try_it: A $200 jacket is 25% off, then an extra 10% off the sale price. Final price?

lessons.title: Unit Pricing and Smart Shopping
concepts: Unit price = total price / quantity: the only fair way to compare different package sizes
12-pack at $8.40 = $0.70 each vs 8-pack at $6.00 = $0.75 each — the bigger pack wins here (not always!)
Watch the units: per ounce vs per pound vs per item — convert to a common unit before comparing
'Sale' is not 'deal': compare the sale unit price against the regular unit price of alternatives

example.code:
12-pack $8.40:  8.40/12 = $0.70 per unit
8-pack $6.00:   6.00/8  = $0.75 per unit
Winner: 12-pack by $0.05/unit
Bulk trap: 24-pack $19.20 = $0.80/unit -- bigger but pricier!
example.walkthrough: Division reveals the truth the packaging hides: the 12-pack's $0.70 beats $0.75. But bulk is not automatically better — the 24-pack at $0.80/unit proves it. The habit: always reduce to per-unit before deciding, and make sure the units match (per oz vs per lb needs a x16 conversion).

pitfalls: Assuming bigger is always cheaper — the bulk trap is real
Comparing per-ounce against per-pound without converting
Ignoring that the 'deal' size might expire or spoil before use
lessons.try_it: Compare: 16 oz at $4.00 vs 12 oz at $3.30. Which is cheaper per ounce?

lessons.title: Budgeting Basics
concepts: A budget allocates income: common framework 50% needs / 30% wants / 20% savings — adjust to reality, but write it down
Pay-yourself-first: move savings out on payday (15% of $3,200 = $480) before spending what remains
Track against the budget monthly: a budget you never review is a wish, not a plan
Emergency fund target: 3-6 months of essential expenses — the shock absorber that keeps debt away

example.code:
$3,200 monthly income, 15% savings:
  Savings = 3200 x 0.15 = $480
  Remaining = 3200 - 480 = $2,720 to allocate
50/30/20 split: needs $1,600 / wants $960 / savings $640
example.walkthrough: The $480 moves first — automation beats willpower. The 50/30/20 split of $3,200 gives concrete caps per category; without caps, 'wants' quietly colonize the savings. Monthly review closes the loop: compare actuals to the plan, adjust the plan (not just the spending) when life changes.

pitfalls: Budgeting what is left after spending — invert it: save first
No monthly review — the budget drifts from reality within weeks
Counting the emergency fund as available savings — it is insurance, not a slush fund
lessons.try_it: On $2,800/month income, compute a 50/30/20 split and the 15% pay-yourself-first amount.

lessons.title: Length: Metric and Imperial
concepts: Metric is base-10: 1 km = 1,000 m, 1 m = 100 cm — conversions are decimal shifts
Key bridges: 1 inch = 2.54 cm, 1 mile = 1.609 km — memorize these two and most conversions follow
Convert by multiplying by the bridge: 26.2 miles x 1.609 = 42.16 km (a marathon)
Dimensional analysis keeps you honest: miles x (km/mile) = km — units cancel like fractions

example.walkthrough: The marathon conversion shows the method: multiply by the bridge factor, cancel the old unit, keep the new one. Writing 'km/mi' as a fraction and canceling 'mi' is dimensional analysis — it catches inverted conversions instantly, because the units will not cancel if you flipped the factor.

pitfalls: Multiplying when you should divide — 42 km is not 16 miles by multiplication
Forgetting bridges are exact-ish: 1.609 vs 1.6 is fine for estimates, not for engineering
Converting twice (miles -> km -> m) in one leap without intermediate checks
lessons.try_it: Convert: 10 km to miles, 72 inches to cm.

lessons.title: Weight and Volume
concepts: Weight bridges: 1 kg = 2.205 lb — kilograms to pounds, multiply; pounds to kilograms, divide
Volume bridges: 1 gallon = 3.785 L; 1 cup = 236.6 mL — cooking and fuel live here
Metric volume is base-10 too: 1 L = 1,000 mL, so 2.5 L = 2,500 mL by decimal shift
Density connects them: 1 mL of water = 1 g — the metric system's elegant anchor

example.walkthrough: Each conversion is one multiplication by the bridge factor. The direction check: kilograms are bigger than pounds, so 2.5 kg must become MORE than 2.5 in pounds (5.51) — if your answer is smaller, you divided. This 'bigger/smaller' sanity check catches most conversion errors before they matter.

pitfalls: Pounds-to-kg by multiplying — direction errors are the #1 conversion mistake
Mixing weight and volume (liters vs kilograms) without density
Fluid ounces vs weight ounces — same word, different units
lessons.try_it: Convert: 10 lb to kg, 2 gallons to liters.

lessons.title: Time Calculations
concepts: Elapsed time: borrow 60 minutes like borrowing in subtraction — 2:20 PM minus 9:45 AM needs care
Convert to 24-hour or minutes-since-midnight first: 9:45 AM = 585 min, 2:20 PM = 860 min, difference = 275 min = 4h 35m
AM/PM trap: 12:30 PM is afternoon, 12:30 AM is night — noon and midnight are the confusion points
Time zones and durations: a 3h 15m flight leaving 10:40 AM arrives 1:55 PM — add hours, then minutes, carry 60s

example.code:
9:45 AM -> 2:20 PM:
  9:45 = 585 min after midnight
  2:20 PM = 14:20 = 860 min
  860 - 585 = 275 min = 4 h 35 m
Shift 11:00 PM -> 7:00 AM = 8 hours (across midnight)
example.walkthrough: Minutes-since-midnight turns clock arithmetic into plain subtraction — no borrowing, no AM/PM traps. Across midnight, add 24h to the end time first. The 11 PM to 7 AM shift: 7:00 AM is 420 min, plus 1440 (next day) = 1860, minus 1380 (11 PM) = 480 min = 8 hours.

pitfalls: Subtracting 9:45 from 2:20 directly — borrow errors and AM/PM mixups
Forgetting midnight crossings in overnight durations
12:00 AM/PM confusion — noon is PM, midnight is AM
lessons.try_it: Find the elapsed time: 8:15 AM to 3:50 PM; 10:30 PM to 6:15 AM.

lessons.title: Temperature Conversion
concepts: F = C x 9/5 + 32 and C = (F - 32) x 5/9 — the two formulas, and the 32 offset is what everyone forgets
Anchor points: 0 C = 32 F (freezing), 100 C = 212 F (boiling), 20 C = 68 F (room), 37 C = 98.6 F (body)
Estimate first: double C and add 30 approximates F (20 C -> 70 F, close to 68) — good for sanity checks

example.walkthrough: Subtract 32 BEFORE multiplying by 5/9 — the offset comes off first because the scales are offset AND stretched. The -40 crossover is a fun check of the formulas: plug -40 into either and you get -40 out. Anchor points (freezing/boiling/body) catch formula errors: if your 'room temperature' answer is 161 F, you forgot the 32.

pitfalls: Multiplying by 9/5 before subtracting 32 — order matters
°C to °F using 5/9 — the fractions swap with direction
No sanity check — 22 C is pleasant, 222 C is an oven
lessons.try_it: Convert: 100 F to C, 30 C to F, using anchor points to verify.

lessons.title: Area and Volume Conversions
concepts: Linear conversions square for area: 1 ft = 12 in, but 1 sq ft = 144 sq in — the factor squares too
Yards: 1 yd = 3 ft, so 1 sq yd = 9 sq ft — divide square feet by 9 for square yards
Room 12 ft x 15 ft = 180 sq ft = 20 sq yd of carpet (180/9)
Acres for land: 1 acre = 43,560 sq ft — a football field is about 1.3 acres

example.code:
12 ft x 15 ft = 180 sq ft
180 sq ft / 9 = 20 sq yd
1 m^2 = 10.76 sq ft (1 m = 3.28 ft, squared)
Paint: 1 gallon covers ~350 sq ft
example.walkthrough: The critical insight: converting the linear factor is not enough — area needs the SQUARED factor. Dividing 180 sq ft by 3 (the linear factor) gives 60, wrong; dividing by 9 (3^2) gives the right 20 sq yd. When an area conversion looks 3x off, you used the linear factor; 9x off, you went the wrong direction.

pitfalls: Dividing square feet by 3 instead of 9 — the linear-factor trap
Forgetting whether the answer should be bigger or smaller — sq yd are bigger units, so fewer of them
Mixing sq ft and linear ft in the same computation
lessons.try_it: A 9 ft x 12 ft room: square feet? Square yards? Gallons of paint at 350 sq ft/gal?

lessons.title: Keywords: English to Math
concepts: 'Sum/total/combined' = add; 'difference/fewer' = subtract; 'product/twice/of' = multiply; 'quotient/per' = divide
'Is' almost always means '=': 'twice a number plus 7 is 31' becomes 2n + 7 = 31
'Less than' reverses order: '5 less than x' is x - 5, NOT 5 - x — the trap is deliberate
Define the variable in words first: 'let n = the number' — unnamed variables produce unanswerable equations

example.code:
'Twice a number plus 7 is 31':
  let n = the number
  2n + 7 = 31
  2n = 24  ->  n = 12
'5 less than twice n is 19': 2n - 5 = 19 -> n = 12
example.walkthrough: Translation is mechanical once the keywords are mapped: 'twice a number' = 2n, 'plus 7' = +7, 'is' = =, '31' = 31. The 'less than' reversal is the classic: '5 less than twice n' reads left-to-right as 5 - 2n (wrong) but means 2n - 5. Defining n in words first keeps the final answer interpretable — 'n = 12' means nothing until you know n is the number.

pitfalls: '5 less than x' as 5 - x — the reversal trap
Skipping the variable definition — solving for a mystery
'Is' translated as anything but '='
lessons.try_it: Translate: 'the quotient of a number and 4, decreased by 3, is 11.' Then solve.

lessons.title: Multi-Step Problems
concepts: Break into stages: read, list knowns/unknowns, translate each relationship, solve, check against the story
Rates: distance = rate x time — 60 mph for 3.5 hours = 210 miles; units multiply just like numbers
Check the answer in the ORIGINAL story, not just the equation — 210 miles in 3.5 h at 60 mph makes sense
Estimate first: 60 x 3.5 ≈ 60 x 3 + 30 = 210 — the estimate IS the check

example.code:
Train at 60 mph for 3.5 hours:
  d = r x t = 60 x 3.5 = 210 miles
Check: 60 mph x 3 h = 180, plus 0.5 h x 60 = 30 -> 210 ✓
Units: (miles/hour) x hours = miles ✓
example.walkthrough: The unit check is free verification: miles/hour times hours cancels to miles, confirming the setup. Breaking 3.5 into 3 + 0.5 makes the mental math exact (180 + 30). The story-check at the end ('does 210 miles feel right for 3.5 hours at highway speed?') catches setup errors no algebra can.

pitfalls: Solving the equation but never checking the story
Unit mismatch: hours x minutes without converting
One giant leap instead of stages — errors hide in leaps
lessons.try_it: A car drives 45 mph for 2 hours 20 minutes. Distance? (Watch the units.)

lessons.title: Work and Rate Problems
concepts: Combined rates add: if A does 1/6 of a job per hour and B does 1/3, together they do 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 per hour
Time together = 1 / (combined rate): 1 / (1/2) = 2 hours — the harmonic pattern
Convert 'hours per job' to 'jobs per hour' first — rates add, times do not
Sanity: together must be faster than the fastest alone (2h < 3h here) — if not, the setup is wrong

example.code:
A: 6 h alone -> rate 1/6 per hour
B: 3 h alone -> rate 1/3 per hour
Combined: 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 per hour
Time = 1 / (1/2) = 2 hours
example.walkthrough: The key move is inverting time to rate: '6 hours per job' becomes '1/6 job per hour', and rates add. The harmonic result (2h) is less than either alone — the sanity check that validates the setup. Adding the times (9h) is the folk error; rates are the additive quantity, never durations.

pitfalls: Adding times instead of rates — 6 + 3 = 9 is always wrong here
Forgetting to invert back to time at the end
No sanity check — together slower than alone means broken setup
lessons.try_it: Two pipes fill a tank in 4h and 6h alone. Together?

lessons.title: Age and Consecutive-Integer Problems
concepts: Consecutive integers: n, n+1, n+2 — 'sum to 87' gives 3n + 3 = 87, so n = 28: 28, 29, 30
Age problems anchor on 'now': let s = son's age now; 'in 5 years' adds 5 to BOTH ages
Maria is 3x her son; in 5 years she is 2x: 3s + 5 = 2(s + 5) -> s = 5, Maria = 15
Always answer the asked question: solving s = 5 when asked for Maria's age (15) loses the point

example.code:
Consecutive integers sum to 87:
  n + (n+1) + (n+2) = 87
  3n + 3 = 87 -> 3n = 84 -> n = 28
  Answer: 28, 29, 30 (largest: 30)
Ages: 3s + 5 = 2(s+5) -> 3s + 5 = 2s + 10 -> s = 5
example.walkthrough: Consecutive integers are one variable in disguise (n, n+1, n+2) — never use three variables. Age problems: the '+5 years' applies to everyone, which is where most setups break (adding 5 to only one side). And the final discipline: re-read the question before answering — the work found s = 5, but 'Maria's age' is 15.

pitfalls: Three variables for consecutive integers — one variable does it
Adding 'in 5 years' to only one person's age
Answering with the intermediate variable instead of the asked quantity
lessons.try_it: Three consecutive even integers sum to 54. Find them. (Hint: n, n+2, n+4.)

lessons.title: Mixture Problems
concepts: Mixtures conserve value: (amount1 x price1) + (amount2 x price2) = total x blend price
One variable suffices: x lb of $4 coffee, (10 - x) lb of $7, blend 10 lb at $5.50/lb
Equation: 4x + 7(10 - x) = 55 -> 70 - 3x = 55 -> x = 5 lb of the $4 coffee
Check reasonableness: blend $5.50 sits between $4 and $7, closer to middle — 5/5 split makes sense

example.code:
$4/lb and $7/lb coffee, 10 lb at $5.50/lb:
  4x + 7(10-x) = 10 x 5.50 = 55
  4x + 70 - 7x = 55
  -3x = -15 -> x = 5 lb of $4 coffee (5 lb of $7)
example.walkthrough: The (10 - x) substitution keeps it one-variable: whatever is not $4 coffee must be $7 coffee. The blend price ($55 total) anchors the equation. The reasonableness check is powerful: $5.50 is midway between $4 and $7, so a 50/50 split (5 and 5) is exactly what you expect — if the math gave 9 and 1, you would recheck.

pitfalls: Two variables with no total constraint — use (total - x)
Forgetting the blend price multiplies by total weight
No reasonableness check — absurd splits pass unnoticed
lessons.try_it: Mix $3/lb and $8/lb nuts for 20 lb at $5/lb. How much of each?

lessons.title: Reading Bar Charts
concepts: Bars encode values by height/length: read each bar's value against the axis, then compare
Totals and differences come from the values, not the visuals: sum the five daily bars for the week
Watch the axis: bars starting at non-zero exaggerate differences — check where the axis begins
Rankings are instant (tallest = max), but exact values need the axis labels

example.code:
Daily sales ($k): Mon 120, Tue 150, Wed 90, Thu 180, Fri 200
Total = 120+150+90+180+200 = 740
Best day: Friday (200)
Tue vs Wed gap: 150 - 90 = 60
example.walkthrough: Read each bar's labeled value first — never eyeball heights for exact numbers. The total (740) is arithmetic on the labels, not area estimation. Friday's bar is tallest (max), and the Tue-Wed gap (60) is a subtraction, not a visual guess. If the y-axis started at 100 instead of 0, Wednesday's bar would look half of Tuesday's while actually being 60% — always check the axis origin.

pitfalls: Eyeballing values instead of reading labels
Ignoring a truncated axis — visual ratios lie when axes do not start at zero
Confusing bar height ratios with value ratios on broken axes
lessons.try_it: From the sales data above: mean daily sales? Worst day?

lessons.title: Line Graphs and Trends
concepts: Line graphs show change over time: slope between points is the rate of change
Read values at the marked points, then subtract for the change: noon 76 F minus 6 AM 58 F = 18 F rise
Steeper segments mean faster change — the steepest part of the curve is where action happened
Flat segments are information too: no change is a finding, not a gap

example.code:
Temperature: 6 AM 58 F, noon 76 F, 6 PM 70 F
Morning rise: 76 - 58 = 18 F
Afternoon drop: 76 - 70 = 6 F
Steepest change: morning (18 F over 6 h = 3 F/hour)
example.walkthrough: Subtract marked values for exact changes: the 18 F morning rise dwarfs the 6 F afternoon drop. Rate = change/time: 3 F per hour in the morning. The steepest segment (morning) is where the story is — line graphs are read for slopes, not just points.

pitfalls: Reading the highest point as the 'change' — change is a difference
Ignoring the time axis scale — 18 F over 6 hours vs 6 F over 6 hours differ in rate
Interpolating between sparse points as if exact
lessons.try_it: A stock goes 100 -> 130 -> 115 over two days. Daily changes? Steepest?

lessons.title: Pie Charts and Proportions
concepts: Pie slices are fractions of a whole: 40% of 250 surveyed = 0.40 x 250 = 100 people
The whole must be known or derivable: percentages alone cannot give counts without the total
Compare slices by percentage, not visual angle — 3D pies distort angles badly
Check the total: slices should sum to 100% — if not, something is off or 'other' is hiding

example.code:
Survey 250 people, 40% prefer X:
  0.40 x 250 = 100 people
Two slices 30% + 25%: combined 55%
Missing slice: 100% - (30+25+40)% = 5%
example.walkthrough: Percent-of-total is the only operation: convert the percent to a decimal, multiply by the total. Without the total (250), '40%' is just a shape — counts need the base. The missing-slice check (slices sum to 100%) catches chart errors and hidden 'other' categories before you quote a number.

pitfalls: Quoting counts from percents without the total
Trusting 3D pie angles over the labeled percentages
Forgetting slices must sum to 100%
lessons.try_it: A budget pie: 35% labor, 25% materials, 15% overhead. What is missing, and what percent?

lessons.title: Tables: Extract and Compute
concepts: Tables reward systematic reading: identify rows, columns, and units before computing anything
Greatest increase = largest positive difference between consecutive entries — compute each, then compare
Averages from tables: sum the column, divide by the count — show the total as an intermediate
Two-series tables: compute each series' change separately, then compare the changes

example.code:
Monthly units: Jan 120, Feb 150, Mar 140, Apr 200, May 210
Changes: +30, -10, +60, +10 -> greatest: April (+60)
Quarterly revenue: 300, 450, 375, 525
Total = 1650; average = 1650/4 = 412.5
example.walkthrough: The differences (+30, -10, +60, +10) make 'greatest increase' mechanical — April's +60 wins. For the quarterly average, the total (1650) is the checkable intermediate: 1650/4 = 412.5. Two-series comparison (store A +60 vs store B +90) follows the same pattern: change per series, then compare changes — never compare endpoints alone.

pitfalls: Picking the max value instead of the max increase
Averaging without showing the total — unverifiable
Comparing endpoints across series instead of comparing changes

lessons.title: Spotting Misleading Graphs
concepts: Truncated y-axis: bars starting at 50 make a 54-vs-50 difference look like doubling — check the origin
Cherry-picked ranges: a 'soaring' line over 3 hand-picked months may be flat over 3 years — ask for the wider window
Area/volume distortion: doubling a bar's height AND width quadruples its area for a 2x value — pictographs lie
Missing baselines: 'up 200%' needs the starting value — 200% of tiny is still tiny

example.code:
Bars: 50 vs 54, axis starts at 48
  Visual: the 54 bar looks ~3x taller
  Reality: 54/50 = 1.08, an 8% difference
Always read the axis numbers, not the ink
example.walkthrough: The 8% reality vs 3x visual is the whole lesson: ink lies, numbers do not. Any chart that hides its axis origin, cherry-picks its window, or scales area instead of length is selling an impression, not information. The defense is always the same — read the numbers, recompute the claim.

pitfalls: Trusting visual impressions over axis labels
Accepting 'up X%' without the baseline
Sharing the chart before checking its honesty

lessons.title: Rounding and Compatible Numbers
concepts: Round to friendly numbers, compute, then adjust: 48 x 21 ≈ 50 x 20 = 1000 (actual 1008 — within 1%)
Compatible numbers are chosen to divide cleanly: 8,432 / 9 ≈ 8,100 / 9 = 900 (actual 937)
Round one up and one down when you can — the errors partially cancel: 48(up) x 21(down)
Estimation is for decisions, not precision: 'about a thousand' is enough to order materials or catch a 10x error

example.walkthrough: Each estimate rounds to numbers the brain divides cleanly: 50x20, 300+500+200, 8100/9. The errors are small (under 4%) because rounding up on one factor and down on the other cancels partially. The point is never the exact answer — it is a number in seconds that brackets the truth and exposes decimal disasters.

pitfalls: Over-rounding both factors the same direction — errors compound instead of canceling
Reporting the estimate as the answer — estimates bracket, they do not replace
Compatible numbers that are not actually compatible — 8,437/9 helps nobody

lessons.title: Front-End Estimation
concepts: Front-end: keep the leading digits, drop the rest — 4,782 + 3,195 + 6,041 ≈ 4,000 + 3,000 + 6,000 = 13,000
Adjust with the dropped parts if needed: the dropped 782 + 195 + 41 ≈ 1,000, refining to ~14,000
Front-end shines for addition/subtraction of big numbers — one pass, leading digits only
Use it for quick quotes: 'about thirteen thousand' wins the bid conversation before the spreadsheet loads

example.walkthrough: The front-end pass takes seconds and lands within 8%; the refinement (adding the dropped leading chunks) nails it exactly here. For multiplication, front-end means leading-digit products with zero-counting: 4,782 x 3,195 ≈ 5,000 x 3,000 = 15,000,000 — count the zeros carefully, that is where front-end multiplication bites.

pitfalls: Dropping digits without noting magnitude — 4,782 becoming 4 instead of 4,000
Zero-counting errors in front-end multiplication
Refining past the point of usefulness — know when to stop
lessons.try_it: Front-end estimate 7,654 + 2,345 + 8,901, then refine.

lessons.title: Estimating with Percents
concepts: Anchor on 10%: move the decimal one place — 10% of 450 = 45, then scale
18% of 450 ≈ 20% of 450 = 90 (actual 81) — round the percent to a friendly one
Percent estimates guard calculator work: if the machine says 810 for 18% of 450, the estimate (90) screams decimal error

example.walkthrough: The 10% anchor plus friendly rounding handles nearly every percent estimate: 18% becomes 20%, 7% becomes 'a bit under 10%'. The 33%-as-one-third trick is exact enough for decisions. The real job of these estimates is guarding exact computation — a 10x decimal slip cannot survive next to a sane estimate.

pitfalls: Computing the exact value when the estimate was the assignment — match effort to need
Anchoring on 1% for big percents — 10% is the better anchor
No guard estimate before trusting calculator output

lessons.title: Reasonableness Checks
concepts: Every computed answer faces the reasonableness court: right magnitude? right sign? right units?
Decimal placement: 12 x 15 = 180 — a calculator saying 1,800 or 18 failed the magnitude check
Sign check: costs cannot be negative, probabilities cannot exceed 1, areas cannot be negative
Unit check: an area in feet, a speed in hours, a percent over 100 where impossible — units testify

example.code:
12 x 15 = 180, not 1,800 (estimate: 10 x 15 = 150)
3.75 x 2.4 = 9.00, not 90.0 (estimate: 4 x 2.4 = 9.6)
P(event) = 1.4  ->  impossible, recheck
Area = -12 sq ft  ->  impossible, sign error
example.walkthrough: Each check is a one-second gate: magnitude (estimate nearby?), sign (possible?), units (correct kind?). The calculator is a fast idiot — it multiplies exactly what you typed, including your typos. Reasonableness is the human's job and the cheapest error-catching system ever invented.

pitfalls: Trusting calculator output without a glance — the machine has no judgment
Checking the arithmetic but not the setup — right math on the wrong problem
Skipping checks under time pressure — pressure is when checks matter most
lessons.try_it: For each: 25 x 40 = ?, 8% of 250 = ?, 7/8 as decimal = ? — estimate, compute, check.

lessons.title: Estimation in Operations
concepts: Quote fast, refine later: 'about $900 in materials' wins the conversation; the $912.40 comes with the purchase order
Sanity-check every spreadsheet total: does the monthly sum sit near 30x the daily average?
Fermi-style breakdowns: how many tiles for the lobby? (area / tile area) x waste factor — rough inputs, useful output
Teach the team: a culture that estimates catches the $10,000 typo before it ships

pitfalls: False precision in quotes — '$912.40' before the job is measured
No waste/contingency factor — exact estimates are exactly wrong

lessons.title: Mental Math Strategies
concepts: Break numbers apart: 48 x 21 = 48 x 20 + 48 = 960 + 48 = 1008 — distribution beats brute force
Compensate after rounding: 297 + 512 = 300 + 512 - 3 = 809 — round, compute, adjust
Doubling and halving: 16 x 25 = 8 x 50 = 400 — scale one factor down, the other up
Left-to-right arithmetic: add the big chunks first (400 + 300), then the details — the answer takes shape early

example.walkthrough: Each strategy replaces a hard computation with an easy one plus a correction: distribution, compensation, and scaling are the big three. The left-to-right habit means you know the answer's magnitude after the first step — errors get caught while there is still time to fix them.

pitfalls: Brute-forcing every computation digit by digit — slow and error-prone
Rounding without compensating — the correction is the strategy
Right-to-left-only arithmetic — no early sense of the answer's size
lessons.try_it: Compute mentally: 52 x 11, 198 + 476, 24 x 5 — naming the strategy each time.

lessons.title: Estimation as a Safety Net
concepts: Estimate BEFORE computing exactly: the estimate brackets the truth and vetoes absurd outputs
Round to one or two significant figures for the estimate — more precision defeats the purpose
Every calculator result faces the estimate: 12 x 15 = 1800 fails against the 150-180 bracket
Estimation is a professional skill, not a shortcut: engineers and analysts estimate constantly to stay oriented

example.code:
Before: 48 x 21 -> ~50 x 20 = ~1,000
Compute: 1,008
Check: 1,008 sits inside the bracket ✓
Before: 8,432 / 9 -> ~9,000/9 = ~1,000
Compute: 937 ✓ inside bracket
example.walkthrough: The three-beat rhythm — estimate, compute, check — takes seconds and catches the errors that cost real money: decimal slips, extra zeros, inverted operations. Professionals do this reflexively; assessments reward it because workplaces depend on it.

pitfalls: Computing first, estimating never — the net is never deployed
Estimates so coarse they cannot veto anything ('between 0 and a million')
Ignoring a failed check — the bracket disagreed, so the computation is guilty until proven innocent

lessons.title: Test-Day Tactics for Math Assessments
concepts: Three passes: easy questions first (bank points), mediums second, hard/unknowns last — never leave blanks
Eliminate before you solve: wrong answers are often designed to be visibly wrong (bad units, absurd magnitude)
Plug-in verification: multiple choice lets you test answers in the equation — sometimes faster than solving
Time budget per question: total time / questions, minus a 10% buffer — when the budget expires, guess and move

example.code:
The 3-pass method:
  Pass 1 (40%): everything you know cold
  Pass 2 (40%): flagged mediums, full work
  Pass 3 (20%): educated guesses on the rest
Elimination: cross out 2 wrong choices first, then decide between survivors
example.walkthrough: Elimination plus estimation solves many questions without full computation: if three choices fail the magnitude check, the fourth wins by logic. Plug-in shines on equations — testing x = 10 in 4x - 11 = 29 takes seconds. The time budget prevents the classic failure: ten minutes on one hard question while five easy ones expire.

pitfalls: Solving every question the long way — elimination and estimation are legitimate tools
No time budget — one tar pit question eats the whole section
Changing answers without new evidence — first instinct after study is usually right
lessons.try_it: Do a 10-question timed set using 3-pass + elimination; log what worked.

lessons.title: Factors, Multiples, and Divisibility
concepts: Factors divide evenly: factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 — find them in pairs (1x12, 2x6, 3x4)
Multiples are the times-table extended: multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24... — infinite upward
Divisibility shortcuts: by 2 (even), by 3 (digits sum to multiple of 3), by 5 (ends 0/5), by 9 (digits sum to multiple of 9), by 10 (ends 0)
GCD is the biggest shared factor (GCD of 12 and 18 is 6); LCM is the smallest shared multiple (LCM of 4 and 6 is 12)

example.walkthrough: The digit-sum test answers divisibility-by-3 in seconds: 15 is a multiple of 3, so 4,821 is too. GCD via factor lists is foolproof at this scale; LCM via multiple lists likewise. These tools power fraction simplification (divide by GCD) and common denominators (use LCM) — they are the machinery behind the fraction work.

pitfalls: Listing factors unsystematically and missing pairs
Confusing GCD (smaller or equal) with LCM (larger or equal)
Testing divisibility by long division — the shortcuts exist for a reason
lessons.try_it: Find GCD(24, 36) and LCM(5, 8); test 7,105 and 9,412 for divisibility by 3 and 5.

lessons.title: Exponents and Scientific Notation
concepts: Scientific notation = a number between 1 and 10 times a power of 10: 0.00045 = 4.5 x 10^-4
The exponent counts decimal moves: small numbers get negative exponents, large numbers positive — 72,000 = 7.2 x 10^4
Multiplying: multiply the coefficients, add the exponents — (2 x 10^3)(3 x 10^2) = 6 x 10^5
Assessment trap: 45 x 10^-5 is NOT scientific notation (45 > 10) — normalize to 4.5 x 10^-4

example.walkthrough: Count the decimal moves and sign the exponent by direction: right moves (small numbers) go negative, left moves (big numbers) go positive. Multiplication keeps the laws of exponents working for you. The normalization rule (coefficient between 1 and 10) is what multiple-choice tests probe — 45 x 10^-5 equals the right value but is not the right FORM.

pitfalls: Positive exponent for small numbers — direction decides the sign
Leaving 45 x 10^-5 un-normalized and picking it as 'scientific notation'
Adding exponents when multiplying coefficients — operations stay in their lanes
lessons.try_it: Write in scientific notation: 0.0000072, 5,900,000; multiply (4 x 10^2)(2 x 10^-3).

lessons.title: Coordinate Plane Basics
concepts: The plane has four quadrants: I (+,+), II (-,+), III (-,-), IV (+,-) — signs in order, counterclockwise from top-right
Plot (x, y): x moves horizontally, y vertically — (-3, 4) sits in quadrant II
Distance between points: the Pythagorean theorem in disguise — d = sqrt((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2
Midpoint: average the coordinates — midpoint of (0,0) and (6,8) is (3, 4)

example.code:
Point (-3, 4): x negative, y positive -> Quadrant II
Distance (0,0) to (3,4): sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5
Midpoint of (0,0),(6,8): ((0+6)/2, (0+8)/2) = (3, 4)
example.walkthrough: Distance is Pythagoras with legs (x2-x1) and (y2-y1): the 3-4-5 triple appears constantly, so (0,0)-(3,4) = 5 should be instant. Midpoint is just two averages. Quadrant signs are the fast check on plotted work — a point you computed as (-3, 4) landing in quadrant IV means a sign slipped.

pitfalls: (x, y) plotted as (y, x) — order matters
Quadrant signs from memory instead of the (+,+), (-,+) pattern
Distance without the final square root
lessons.try_it: Plot (-2, -5), (4, 1): quadrants? Distance between them? Midpoint?

simulations.title: The SLA budget
simulations.brief: Sales promises 99.9% uptime. Convert the nines to minutes, audit last quarter, and enforce the budget.

steps.symptom: Sales promises 99.9% uptime. How many minutes of downtime does that allow per 30-day month?
steps.explain: 0.1% of 43,200 = 43.2 minutes. The nines table: 99% = 7.2h, 99.9% = 43.2m, 99.99% = 4.32m per month.

steps.symptom: Last quarter you burned 60 minutes. What was the actual uptime?
steps.explain: (129,600 − 60) / 129,600 = 99.9537%. You missed three nines by 16.8 minutes.

steps.symptom: The error budget is nearly spent with a week left. Policy?
options: Freeze non-essential deploys until the budget resets — the budget is a throttle, not a suggestion
steps.explain: Error budgets exist to pace risk. Spending the last 10% on a risky deploy gambles the SLA for no reason.

simulations.debrief: SLA math is subtraction with consequences: convert the nines to minutes, track the burn, and let the budget throttle risk.

simulations.title: The unit conversion
simulations.brief: A 2.5 TB backup, a 100 Mbps link, and an interviewer watching your units. Estimate the transfer.

steps.symptom: The backup is 2.5 TB. The upload link is 100 Mbps. How long, roughly?
steps.explain: 20,000,000 Mb / 100 Mbps = 200,000 s ≈ 55.6 h. Bytes-to-bits (×8) is where every estimate dies.

steps.symptom: Same backup; the link is now 1 Gbps and protocol overhead eats 10%.
steps.explain: 20,000,000 / 900 ≈ 22,222 s ≈ 6.17 h. Overhead is a divisor on throughput, not a rounding error.

steps.symptom: The interviewer asks for the rule of thumb.
options: Bits = bytes × 8, then divide by effective throughput — and always ask about overhead
steps.explain: The whole discipline is unit hygiene: bytes to bits, advertised to effective, then divide.

simulations.debrief: Transfer math: ×8 for bits, ÷ by real (not advertised) throughput, and overhead is never zero.

simulations.title: Shift coverage
simulations.brief: Staff a 24/7 desk: shifts per day, analysts per week, buffer for reality. Show the arithmetic.

steps.symptom: Cover a 24/7 desk with 8-hour shifts. Minimum headcount per day, ignoring days off?
steps.explain: 24 / 8 = 3. That is the floor before weekends, PTO, and sick cover multiply it.

steps.symptom: Each analyst works 5 days a week. Weekly shift-slots needed?
steps.explain: 21 / 5 = 4.2, and you cannot hire 0.2 of a person — always round up, then add coverage margin.

steps.symptom: Add 20% buffer for PTO and sick. Final number?
steps.explain: 5 × 1.2 = 6. Staffing math always rounds up: the buffer is the difference between covered and paged.

simulations.debrief: Staffing is division with round-ups: slots per day, slots per week, then buffer — never round people down.

simulations.title: Reorder point
simulations.brief: The depot burns through SSDs. Compute the reorder point, stress it, and name where the formula breaks.

steps.symptom: The depot uses 40 SSDs a day. Lead time is 5 days. Reorder point with no safety stock?
steps.explain: 40 × 5 = 200. Order when stock hits 200 and the shipment lands as you hit zero — in a perfect world.

steps.symptom: Usage spikes to 60/day during refresh cycles. Add safety stock for the spike across the lead time.
steps.explain: 60 × 5 = 300. Safety stock is just the reorder math re-run at the stressed rate.

options: When demand or lead time varies — then you model the variance, not the average
steps.explain: Averages lie under variance. Real reorder math uses the distribution of demand and lead time, not their means.

simulations.debrief: Inventory math: daily rate × lead time, re-run at the stressed rate, and distrust averages.

simulations.title: Throughput sizing
simulations.brief: Size the API fleet for peak, project a year of growth, and defend the headroom to Finance.

steps.symptom: The API serves 800 req/s at peak. One server handles 200 req/s. Servers needed at 70% max utilization?
steps.explain: Effective capacity per server: 200 × 0.7 = 140. 800 / 140 = 5.71 → 6. Headroom is a divisor, then round up.

steps.symptom: Traffic grows 15% per quarter. Servers needed in a year at the same headroom?
steps.explain: 1399 / 140 = 9.99 → 10. Compounding turns 15% into 75% — linear intuition underbuys.

steps.symptom: Finance asks why not run at 95% utilization instead.
options: Queueing theory: at high utilization any burst becomes a queue — latency, not throughput, is the constraint
steps.explain: Throughput is flat until saturation; latency is not. The 70% target buys latency headroom, not idle vanity.

simulations.debrief: Capacity math: divide by effective (not nameplate) capacity, compound the growth, and buy latency headroom.

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.
